articles.title: Russia shows off new laser weapon against drones
articles.body:
- A Russian military blogger published footage claiming a Russian laser weapon system has destroyed several hundred Ukrainian drones near strategic sites in southwestern Russia.
- The claims, including a planned second-generation system for intercepting aircraft and cruise missiles, have not been independently verified.
Footage circulating in Russian pro-military channels this week shows what is claimed to be a Russian laser weapon system engaging aerial drones, according to a Russian military blogger who described the video as an “exclusive.”
The blogger’s post claimed several such systems are now protecting strategic sites in southwestern Russia and that the laser complexes have destroyed several hundred Ukrainian drones. The claim has not been independently verified, and no Russian government or military agency has confirmed the figures.
“Only we have sensational footage of the destruction of Ukrainian drones in the sky by a combat Russian laser complex,” the blogger wrote. “Several of these laser installations now cover our strategic facilities in the southwest of the country.”
Based on the footage, the system appears to be a containerized platform combining a laser weapon, a targeting and guidance system, and a command post where an operator controls the unit. The system reportedly includes its own detection setup for tracking aerial threats, combining radar and visual sensors, according to the footage.
The blogger’s post also claimed developers are preparing a second-generation version of the system, intended to intercept faster targets, including tactical aircraft and cruise missiles.
“I am not inclined to overestimate this innovative type of weapon based on ‘new physical principles,’ but combined with traditional air defense systems, a combat laser will definitely be useful for protecting the country from air raids,” the blogger wrote. “It is also gratifying that we not only have such combat ‘purple beams,’ but they have also proven their effectiveness. Now these ‘Jedi swords’ need to be developed and constantly improved. Such is the path.”
Directed energy weapons for counter-drone use have drawn increasing interest from multiple militaries in recent years, though publicly verified operational combat use against drone swarms remains limited across all countries developing the technology. Laser weapons face documented limitations including reduced effectiveness in poor weather, atmospheric interference over longer ranges, and thermal management requirements for sustained operation.
The claims made in the Russian footage, including the number of drones destroyed, the specific location of the systems, and the timeline for a second-generation variant, have not been corroborated by independent sources or confirmed by official Russian military statements.

articles.title: Poland intercepts Russian spy plane over Baltic Sea again
articles.body:
- Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea on Monday, 30 kilometers north of Łeba.
- Poland's defense minister said the aircraft did not violate Polish airspace, in at least the third such intercept reported this year.
Polish fighter jets intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft over the Baltic Sea on Monday, roughly 30 kilometers (19 miles) north of Łeba on Poland’s coast, Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defense Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said.
“Russia has once again tested our deterrence and air defense systems,” Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote. “Before noon, 30 km north of Łeba, our fighters intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft. There was no violation of our airspace over the Baltic.”
The aircraft did not violate Polish airspace, according to the minister. Monday’s intercept was at least the third publicly reported Il-20 intercept by Polish fighters over the Baltic Sea this year, following similar incidents in March, May and July.
The Il-20, known by NATO as the “Coot-A,” is a Soviet-designed signals and electronic reconnaissance aircraft derived from the Il-18 airliner. Russia regularly flies the aircraft over the Baltic Sea to collect electronic and communications intelligence, and the flights have become a recurring trigger for NATO quick reaction alert sorties in the region.
In several previous intercepts this year, Polish officials said the Il-20 was operating without a filed flight plan and with its transponder switched off. In March, Poland’s Operational Command of the Armed Forces said one such intercept marked the aircraft’s ninth reconnaissance mission of the year in the region, describing the pattern as a sustained Russian intelligence-gathering effort rather than an isolated event.
Poland has used both MiG-29 and F-16 fighters to carry out Il-20 intercepts over the Baltic this year. The MiG-29, a Soviet-designed aircraft, remains in a shrinking quick reaction alert role as Poland phases in newer F-16 and FA-50 fighters, with some retired Polish MiG-29s transferred to Ukraine.
Kosiniak-Kamysz has previously described the Il-20 flights as deliberate provocations intended to test Polish and NATO air defense response times, radar coverage and command-and-control coordination along the alliance’s eastern flank.

articles.title: Israel, Greece sign $3.5 billion air defense deal
articles.body:
- Israel and Greece signed a €3 billion defense export deal called "Achilles Shield" for a multi-layered Israeli-built air defense array.
- The deal includes David's Sling, SPYDER, BARAK MX, MMR radars, a new command system, and a separate €26 million Drone Dome contract.
Israel and Greece signed a defense export agreement worth approximately €3 billion ($3.5 billion) Monday, under which Israel will build Greece a multi-layered air defense array combining several Israeli-made systems, according to a statement from Israel’s Ministry of Defense.
The deal, known in Greece as “Achilles Shield,” is the largest defense export agreement in the history of Israel-Greece relations and one of the largest in Israel’s history, according to the ministry. Israel’s Ministry of Defense Director General, Maj. Gen. (Res.) Amir Baram, signed the agreement with his Greek counterpart, Ioannis Bouras, at a ceremony at the ministry’s headquarters.
The array includes the David’s Sling missile defense system, developed by Israel’s Missile Defense Organization with Rafael as prime developer, along with Rafael’s SPYDER air defense system. It also includes the BARAK MX system, built by Israel Aerospace Industries, and MMR multi-mission radars for air surveillance, manufactured by ELTA Systems, an IAI subsidiary. Rafael will separately develop a new national command and control system intended to integrate the full range of air defense capabilities under the program.
A supplementary contract worth €26 million ($30 million) was signed alongside the main deal for Rafael’s Drone Dome systems, intended to defend strategic sites in Greece against drones.
Greece is the second European country to acquire the David’s Sling system, according to Rafael Chairman Yuval Steinitz. The ministry described the program as the first time it will supply a country with a complete air defense array covering threats ranging from ballistic missiles to hostile drones.
“My visit to Greece a few months ago, as the guest of Greek Defense Minister Dendias, was another expression of the depth of the strategic relationship between Israel and Greece and of our shared determination to keep strengthening it,” said Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz.
“The ‘Achilles Shield’ deal is a strategic milestone in Israel’s defense relationship with Greece, reflecting the deep trust our partners around the world place in Israel’s technological edge and the proven track record of our defense systems in the field,” said Baram.
IAI Chairman Boaz Levy referenced the company’s systems performing during recent fighting against Iran and its proxies.
“IAI’s operational air defense systems proved their capabilities in the recent fighting against Iran and its proxies, successfully intercepting a range of threats, chief among them exo-atmospheric ballistic missiles,” Levy said.
The agreement includes a broader industrial cooperation component. Israel’s Ministry of Defense said it will expand defense industrial cooperation with Greece, including the transfer of knowledge and technology to Greek industry, as part of ongoing government-to-government dialogue between the two countries’ defense ministries.
The Israeli ministry has operated under what it described as an emergency production framework since the outbreak of the war in Gaza, combining output for the Israel Defense Forces with continued exports to partner countries. The ministry attributed part of Greece’s decision to Israeli systems’ battlefield performance during that conflict and the broader regional fighting involving Iran.

articles.title: Pentagon secretly hiring military influencers in social media push – WaPo
articles.body:
Pentagon secretly hiring military influencers in social media push – WaPo
The Pentagon has secretly hired conservative military veterans with a large social media following for undisclosed government roles, The Washington Post reported on Sunday. The influencers have promoted US War Secretary Pete Hegseth’s views while attacking critics of the Trump administration, the newspaper claimed.
The report comes amid President Donald Trump’s push to eliminate what his administration calls “woke” ideology from the military and his longstanding clashes with mainstream media.
According to the Post, those hired include retired Air Force Colonel Rob Maness and retired Army Colonels Kurt Schlichter and Thomas Anderson. Some of their assignments could influence policy, the newspaper claims, citing anonymous sources familiar with the matter.
All three have reportedly received official civilian email accounts and been assigned to the office of Pentagon personnel chief Anthony Tata. His team has been tasked with addressing “culture-war issues,” including reviewing military colleges for “woke” ideology, according to the Post.
The newspaper goes on to cite a late August dispute involving conservative influencer Jennica Pounds as an example of the Pentagon’s social media efforts.
Pounds accused a State Department official of trying to “entrap” her into publishing government secrets as a journalistic scoop. US Undersecretary of State for Public Diplomacy Sarah Rogers later said she had approached Pounds and released the documents herself, prompting the influencer to apologize for “making a public spectacle” of the episode.
The Pentagon tightened press access rules last September as part of a broader crackdown on unauthorized disclosures following reports of turmoil inside the department. It has also reportedly considered using lie detector tests to identify officials leaking information.
Trump and Hegseth have repeatedly clashed with mainstream media over reports based on leaked documents and anonymous sources.
Earlier this month, Trump lashed out over reports that the war on Iran had significantly depleted US stocks of critical missiles and air defense interceptors, insisting no shortage existed.
“The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down. Long term jail sentences will be sought!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Amid suspicion of Russian sabotage, Warsaw eyes link to foreign intelligence services.
Poland has opened a “terror” probe into a fire at a factory supplying parts for drones for Ukraine.
The Polish National Prosecution Office announced the launch of the investigation on Monday. While no details were offered, Russia is widely suspected of running sabotage operations across Europe against facilities supplying Ukraine as it defends itself against Moscow’s invasion.

According to the prosecution statement, the probe has been launched to investigate “participation in the activities of a foreign intelligence service directed against the Republic of Poland and for a terrorist offence, consisting of deliberately causing a fire on the premises of the WB Electronics factory using a device containing flammable materials”.
The WB Electronics factory in Skarzysko-Kamienna, located south of Warsaw, was reported to have caught fire shortly after midnight. The facility manufactures key components for drones which are supplied to the Polish and Ukrainian militaries.
Firefighters spent two hours containing the fire. The country’s Internal Security Agency is assisting the police with the investigation, officials said.
No details have been provided to the public at this stage “due to their specific and confidential nature,” an agency spokesman wrote on social media.
WB Electronics is one of Poland’s largest private defence companies. It manufactures loitering munitions, drones, fire-control systems and military-related communication tools and platforms. The Ukrainian military uses the FlyEye and Warmate drones.
A number of European countries supporting Ukraine have reported incidents that are believed to be sabotage operations by the Russians.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk told reporters in August that a Russian citizen was detained “who had been recruited by Russian services to carry out assassination in Warsaw”.
In another incident, an unexploded drone was discovered at a German airport earlier in August.
Poland has been increasing its security expenditure and military capabilities due to fears of Russian attacks. WB Electronics is a key supplier to the Polish military.

articles.body:
Ukrainians turn anger on Kiev for storing explosives near their homes
Residents of the Kiev suburb of Milaya have accused Ukrainian officials of placing an ammunition depot dangerously close to civilian homes, according to interviews published by The Guardian on Monday.
The military storage site was hit last week during a Russian barrage. The Russian Defense Ministry said the attack targeted a warehouse complex storing components for Ukrainian long-range kamikaze drones used in strikes on logistics and e-commerce facilities in Russia.
Secondary explosions continued for hours after the strike, scattering stored military ordnance around homes just hundreds of meters from the depot, local residents told the British newspaper.
“Those who set up the depot here are to blame. There are people here, this is a village. You can’t keep something like that here,” Vera, 65, reportedly said.
She and her son Sergey spent hours sheltering in a small bunker beside their home as dozens of secondary explosions rocked the area.
“I thought it was humanitarian aid that was stored there,” Sergey told the newspaper.
The incident killed at least 38 people and damaged more than 200 private homes and 14 apartment buildings, the Kiev military administration said on Sunday. Thirty of those killed were residents of a care home located close to the ammunition depot, according to The Guardian.
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky said an investigation had been launched into the “terrible negligence” that allowed munitions to be stored so close to civilians.
“Another such crime – after what happened in Vishnevoe – is absolutely unacceptable,” he wrote on X on Saturday.
A Russian strike on an ammunition depot in the Kiev suburb of Vishnevoe on July 6 also triggered massive secondary explosions, damaging hundreds of civilian buildings and causing civilian casualties. Following that incident, Zelensky and other senior Ukrainian officials vowed to prevent munitions from being stored near residential areas.
Storing ammunition near civilian housing could contravene international humanitarian law. Under Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions, parties to a conflict must, “to the maximum extent feasible,” avoid locating military objectives within or near densely populated areas.

articles.title: Taiwan military aligns more closely with US combat practices
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The US is increasingly influencing Taiwan’s combat tactics and equipment, according to a Business Insider report.
Chieh Chung (揭仲), a senior analyst at the Institute for National Defense and Security Research, told Business Insider that Taiwan is following more US recommendations on training, target identification and strikes, and special forces operations.
"This makes it necessary for the US side to observe live exercises to assess the effectiveness and shortcomings of its recommendations and of bilateral military exchanges, providing a basis for subsequent adjustments and revisions," Chieh said.
This year’s Han Kuang exercises introduced the “backbrief” for the first time, per Business Insider. It is a US military practice in which junior commanders relay their understanding of a mission and its orders to their superiors.
Taiwan is now adopting it as part of efforts to train and authorize lower-level commanders to make their own decisions if communication with superiors is lost.
Lin Ping-yu (林秉宥), New Taipei City councilor and former Taiwanese special forces paratrooper, said, "This highlights an area where Taiwan's military culture urgently needs to evolve," according to Business Insider.
"The traditional mindset of 'mission accomplished at all costs' is ill-suited to modern battlefields," he added.
When asked about US military presence during the Han Kuang exercise, a US State Department spokesperson told Business Insider that the US remains committed to its “one China” policy and to maintaining peace in the Taiwan Strait.
The spokesperson did not confirm if there are military personnel on the ground. However, they said the US helps provide Taiwan with the necessary arms and related support to defend itself.
Some of those weapons were featured during the Han Kuang exercise, including Patriot missiles, M1A2 Abrams tanks, F-16Vs, and High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems, according to Business Insider. Taiwanese troops were also seen launching Anduril’s Altius 600M loitering munitions during drills.
Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey said in June that he hopes to expand manufacturing in Taiwan.
Earlier this month, Taiwan Defense Minister Wellington Koo (顧立雄) said that Taiwan-US military cooperation “is far closer than you might imagine,” per a Wall Street Journal report. “The public sees only the arms sales, but in fact, it’s multifaceted and involves so much more,” he said.
“Through military exchanges, we have been learning so much practical combat experience from the US,” Koo said. However, the defense minister stressed that Taiwan’s plan for a potential cross-strait conflict does not rely on US military intervention, WSJ reported.

articles.title: Voorheis Takes Helm of Life Cycle Management Center with $400B Portfolio
articles.body:
Lt. Gen. Jason D. Voorheis has taken command of the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center, a sprawling organization with a $400 billion portfolio, establishing him as one of the service’s top acquisition officials.
Voorheis moves into the job having jumped the rank of major general. As a one star, he was program acquisition executive for command, control, communications, and battle management, or C3BM, the office overseeing the Air Force’s effort to create a massive “battle network.”
Voorheis assumed command of AFLCMC on Aug. 27 during a ceremony at the National Museum of the U.S. Air Force at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base, Ohio, according to a release.
In his new role, Voorheis will also serve as the PAE for combat readiness and integrating PAE for mission systems.
AFLCMC has more than 21,000 employees and manages acquisition, upgrades, and support for aircraft, engines, munitions, electronics, and cyber systems. In other words, it’s the nerve center of keeping the service’s critical hardware running.
“Just about every aircraft, weapon system, uniform, and piece of gear our Airmen take into harm’s way is acquired, fielded, modernized, and sustained by the expertise within AFLCMC. You are the engine of our nation’s defense,” Voorheis told the center’s personnel at the ceremony.
Voorheis takes the post following the retirement of Lt. Gen. Donna D. Shipton, who also previously worked as the Integrating Program Executive Officer for Mission Systems.
Brig. Gen. Joshua Williams took over Voorheis’ previous role as the head of the C3BM office on Aug. 28, according to a separate release. The Air Force established C3BM in 2022, and Maj. Gen. Luke C.G. Cropsey served as its first commander, followed by Vorheis, who took over in February. Cropsey now serves as the military deputy to the Air Force acquisition executive in the Pentagon.
In bidding farewell to the C3BM office, Voorheis said his six months in the job included some of the “most rewarding experiences throughout my career.”
“The mission ahead does not pause,” Voorheis added. “Never stop challenging legacy processes that slow down capability delivery.”
The main goal of the C3BM office is to create a DAF Battle Network, an integrated system of systems that links sensor, effector, and logistics systems. With about 50 programs of record, it is the DAF’s piece of the Pentagon’s massive Combined Joint All Domain Command and Control effort, which seeks to connect any sensor, shooter, and logistics node to a shared network across all of the services.
But the three-star’s experience isn’t limited to the DAF Battle Network; he previously served as the program executive officer for fighters and advanced aircraft, the materiel leader for the F-15 program office, and system program director for the B-21 bomber, according to his official biography.
AFLCMC stood up in 2012 as part of an effort to consolidate and streamline operations within Air Force Materiel Command. It is one of six centers under AFMC, trimmed from a previous dozen centers the service operated, to lower costs, improve readiness, increase aircraft production, and reduce parts shortages, Air & Space Forces Magazine previously reported.
The other centers under AFMC are the Air Force Research Laboratory, the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center, the Air Force Test Center, the Air Force Installation Management Center, and the Air Force Sustainment Center.

articles.title: Ukraine seeks more drones and air defence from Latvia
articles.body:
Ukraine has asked Latvia to support the rapid delivery of air defence equipment, unmanned ground vehicles, fibre-optic-controlled drones and additional strike capabilities as Kyiv sets out its current battlefield priorities, according to Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence.
Ukrainian Defence Minister Evgeniy Khmara and Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces Mykhailo Drapatyi discussed the requirements during a meeting with Latvian Defence Minister Raivis Melnis, the Ukrainian Ministry of Defence announced on 29 August.
The Ukrainian side identified four areas as priorities: unmanned ground vehicles, fibre-optic-controlled drones, what the ministry described as “middle-strike capabilities”, and air defence assets. Khmara also stressed the need for equipment identified as urgent to reach Ukrainian forces as quickly as possible, making delivery times part of the discussions alongside the type of equipment being sought.
Fibre-optic-controlled drones have taken on a growing battlefield role because the control link is carried through a physical fibre rather than relying on a conventional radio connection. The approach can allow operators to retain control in environments where radio-frequency links are heavily disrupted, although the systems bring their own operational limitations.
Unmanned ground vehicles have similarly been employed for an expanding range of battlefield tasks, including logistics and other activities in areas where exposing personnel carries additional risk. Ukraine has increasingly sought to expand the use of uncrewed systems across land, air and maritime operations.
Air defence remains another continuing requirement for Kyiv as Russian forces employ combinations of missiles and uncrewed attack aircraft against targets across Ukraine. The Ukrainian ministry did not identify particular air defence systems being requested from Latvia in its account of the meeting.
Latvia, meanwhile, intends to continue providing security assistance to Ukraine worth at least 0.25% of its gross domestic product each year. Kyiv said it is also looking to Riga to work with other governments and through multinational initiatives to generate further military assistance. The two defence delegations discussed areas beyond the immediate supply of equipment, including rehabilitation for Ukrainian military personnel, training and the development of cyber capabilities.
Ukraine also offered to share operational experience with Latvia. According to the ministry, this could include lessons from multi-domain operations, territorial defence and the construction and development of modern fortifications.
Latvia has been among the NATO members providing sustained military assistance to Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.

US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigns after 18 months on the job, White House says
No reason was given for Driscoll’s departure but tensions with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth have been widely reported
US Army Secretary Dan Driscoll is stepping down after 18 months on the job, the White House said Monday, in the latest departure of a top military leader during the Trump administration.
No reason was given for the departure of Driscoll, who is a friend of Vice-President J.D. Vance, but tensions with Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth have been widely reported. It marks the latest in a series of shake-ups of top military leadership, with the army especially seeing major upheaval.
“Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more,” White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly said in a statement.
“The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” the statement said.
The Pentagon referred questions to the US Army. The army has not immediately responded to an email seeking comment. A spokesman for Driscoll has not responded to a text message.
Hegseth suddenly ousted the service’s top uniformed leader, General Randy George, in April, while the army’s commander in Europe and Africa, General Christopher Donahue, unexpectedly stepped down in June.
General Christopher LaNeve, who has made a meteoric rise under Hegseth, took George’s place as the army’s acting chief of staff. Under LaNeve, the service is pulling the plug on a drone modernisation programme that Driscoll had heralded. An army unit based in Europe was building its own drones before LaNeve directed it to end its efforts and return to being a traditional infantry battalion, officials said this week.

Ukraine revamps security protocols amid Russian drone strikes aimed at ‘paralysing’ capital
- Kyiv is reviewing security protocols after a surge in Russian drone attacks aimed at disrupting the capital's daily life and economy.
- The city faces frequent air-raid alerts, metro disruptions, and plans for remote learning as safety measures amid ongoing strikes.
- Officials and residents express concern over the effectiveness of current protocols, with recent attacks causing casualties and raising fears for civilian safety.
AI generated
KYIV - Kyiv on Aug 31 announced a review of security protocols – especially for public transport – after a dramatic surge in Russian drone attacks it says are aimed at “paralysing” the Ukrainian capital.
After intensifying its missile strikes on Kyiv earlier this summer, Russia has also drastically increased its daily drone attacks.
Since last week, jet-powered drones have been attacking Kyiv and surrounding areas, triggering a dozen air-raid alerts a day and forcing a partial shutdown of economic activity.
The metro no longer crosses the Dnieper River, which divides the capital in two, causing traffic chaos.
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram he had met with local officials on Aug 31 to discuss changes to security protocols, suggesting one metro line remain open despite strikes.
City hall also announced it was preparing changes for schools, including remote learning, as the school year begins in Ukraine on Sept 1.
Kyiv residents took to social media to question whether it was possible to continue living in the capital, especially with children, with some mulling a move to safer areas.
“The enemy is trying to paralyse economic activity in the capital and major cities,” Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi said on Facebook on Aug 29.
“Prolonged air-raid alerts affect not only people’s safety, but also the operation of businesses, logistics, transportation, schools, kindergartens,” he said.
He called for adapting security rules “with the aim of better protecting people and preserving the ability to live in our cities and communities”.
Some in Kyiv – a city of three million people – consider the security protocols ineffective, with experts suggesting a more flexible approach.
“If, because of a single drone somewhere in the region, everything or almost everything in the entire capital stops for about 40 minutes every hour, we’re not going to last long like this,” Mykhailo Zhernakov, head of a legal think-tank, said on Facebook on Aug 27.
Overnight from Aug 28 to 29, a Russian strike on an ammunition depot killed 38 people in the capital’s suburbs.

Rights groups warn that armed groups are increasingly recruiting children to their ranks through social media.
Three minors were among those killed in a Colombian military air strike on cocaine-trafficking rebels last week, authorities said, as President Abelardo de la Espriella intensifies operations against armed groups.
The August 27 bombing in the southern Guaviare department was the deadliest military operation since de la Espriella took office earlier this month. They also reported that algorithms on platforms including Meta and TikTok “appear to have actively promoted” content encouraging children to join rebel groups.

articles.title: 'What a stupid question': Trump dismisses use of nuclear weapon against Iran
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump dismissed the possibility of using a nuclear weapon against Iran when questioned by a reporter on Monday.
“Have you ruled out using a nuclear weapon against Iran?” the reporter asked.
“They’re totally defeated militarily, so I defeat them, and now I should use a nuclear weapon on top of them? What a stupid question,” Trump responded.
Trump previously said in April that he would not use a nuclear weapon against Iran, telling reporters that nuclear weapons “should never be allowed to be used by anybody.”
Trump calls Iran a 'failed nation'
Asked whether the latest developments with Iran were part of a limited campaign or a return to full-scale war, Trump described Iran as a “failed nation.”
“They've got 350 percent inflation. They have no currency. They're not paying their soldiers. Their leaders are largely dead. Their navy is gone. Their air force is gone. Their surveillance equipment is almost entirely gone,” Trump said.
“That doesn't mean we won't smack them. We'll see what happens,” he added.
Trump also addressed the Strait of Hormuz, saying the US had it in “extremely good shape.”
“You know we're taking over many, many ships. Got through last night, as you know, with the navy's assistance. And we've been averaging 30 ships a night. That's a lot. And a lot of oil is coming out,” Trump said.
“That's why you haven't seen the price of oil go like they thought it might have to go,” he added.
Trump has previously tied pressure on Iran to reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier in August, he said the strait would open “very soon” and warned that Iran would be “hit very hard” if it did not.
'Iran will never have a nuclear weapon'
Trump went on to reiterate that preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon remained a central objective.
“Iran will never have a nuclear weapon. See, that's what it's all about. It's not about any of the other things. It's about us as a country and for the world. Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said.
“If Iran had a nuclear weapon, Israel would have been wiped out. You would have no Israel right now, and you'd probably have no Middle East,” he continued.
Trump added that Iran would eventually be “hitting our cities at some point,” before reiterating, “Iran will never have a nuclear weapon.”
Trump has repeatedly maintained that Iran will not be permitted to obtain a nuclear weapon. Earlier in August, he said that Iran “will never have a nuclear weapon” and added that he had “no choice” but to prevent Tehran from obtaining one.

articles.title: Putin to take part in SCO summit, hold bilateral meetings
articles.body:
BISHKEK, September 1. /TASS/. Russian President Vladimir Putin continues his visit to the Kyrgyz capital of Bishkek. His agenda for Tuesday includes events related to the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) and a marathon of bilateral meetings.
SCO summit
The SCO summit will officially begin on the morning of September 1 with a welcoming ceremony for the leaders of the organization’s member states hosted by Kyrgyzstan's President Sadyr Japarov. The leaders will then pose for a photo.
The summit will kick off with a Council of Heads of State meeting themed “25 years of the SCO: together for a stable world, development, and prosperity.” Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov told reporters that the leaders would review the organization's activities in the past 25 years and discuss efforts to further strengthen the SCO and expand cooperation in politics, security, the economy, and humanitarian ties. The SCO leaders will also exchange views on pressing international and regional issues, with a special focus on improving the organization’s effectiveness.
After the SCO session, a traditional SCO+ meeting will be held, bringing together the leaders of SCO observer countries, dialogue partners and guests invited by the chair. This time, the SCO member states - Russia, Belarus, China, India, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Pakistan, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan - will be joined by Afghanistan, Mongolia, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Bahrain, Egypt, Cambodia, Qatar, Kuwait, Laos, the Maldives, Myanmar, Nepal, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Sri Lanka. The meeting will also be attended by the heads of several international organizations, including the United Nations, the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO), and the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS). The broader meeting will be held under the theme "The United Nations as the Key Element of a Fair World Order: The Contribution of SCO+ Countries to the Formation of a Multipolar World," Ushakov said.
The summit will conclude with the signing of more than 20 documents, the main one being the Bishkek Declaration, which will reflect consolidated approaches to pressing regional and international issues, including economic challenges. Another important document is a protocol to the 2002 SCO Charter, which will streamline the structure of the organization’s bodies. The Universal Center for Countering Security Challenges and Threats and the Anti-Drug Center will be added to them. A new "SCO partner" category will also be introduced, aimed at simplifying the organization’s structure by merging the existing observer and partner categories. In addition, a package of decisions on combating drug trafficking, international security, science, technology and logistics is expected to be signed, along with statements on energy efficiency, nuclear safety and security, and cooperation in emergency response.
International communication
Once the SCO summit is over, Putin will continue his series of meetings with other countries’ leaders. He is scheduled to hold talks with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Mongolian President Ukhnaagiin Khurelsukh, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, and Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov.
Putin will sum up the results of his visit by taking questions from Kremlin pool journalists accompanying him on the trip.

articles.title: Air Force Pulls ICBM Testing Device After Finding Likely Carcinogen
articles.body:
The Air Force has pulled a piece of testing equipment for its Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missiles after discovering some appeared to be contaminated with a possible carcinogen.
The order to stop using the AN/PRM-10 test oscillator set came after an Airman discovered polychlorinated biphenyl, or PCB, residue on one of the units during a routine inspection in August, Air Force Global Strike Command said in an Aug. 28 statement.
The Airman, who was at F.E. Warren Air Force Base, Wyo., reported the residue and received medical attention for the exposure before returning to duty, according to the statement
The EPA has concluded PCBs are a probable cause of cancer in humans, as well as having negative immune system, reproductive, developmental, and neurological effects. PCBs were regularly used in electrical, heat transfer, and hydraulic equipment for about 50 years due to the compound’s electrical insulating properties, high boiling point, and nonflammibility, until they were banned in 1979 as evidence grew that the compound was toxic to people and the environment.
The AN/PRM-10 test oscillator set is a signal generator used to examine ICBM communications systems, per the Global Strike Command statement. After the Airman reported the issue and tests confirmed the presence of PCBs on that test unit, the 20th Air Force—which oversees ICBM bases—ordered all AN/PRM-10 kits be inspected.
That review of all AN/PRM-10 kits was done within three days, and officials found potential PCB residue on six of eight systems. Samples collected from those systems are now being tested. Officials also ordered safety warnings, precautions, and mandatory personal protective equipment requirements be updated where other legacy test units are still used.
But all AN/PRM-10 systems have been pulled from use in the 20th, and units are transitioning to a modern replacement tester that is free of PCBs, Air Force Global Strike Command said. Leaders are working with the Minuteman III systems program office to dispose of any existing AN/PRM-10 kits and identify any other test equipment pieces that may have PCBs.
The “20th Air Force takes the responsibility to protect our Airmen very seriously,” Commander Maj. Gen. Colin Connor said in a statement. “As our Airmen are our greatest asset, their safety and health are my top priority.”
Concerns about rates of cancer among missileers and other Airmen who work with ICBMs has grown in recent years. In 2023, the Air Force launched a study dubbed the Missile Community Cancer Study to review the possibility of clusters of non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma at ICBM bases, as well as other specific cancer concerns raised by the community.
The Torchlight Initiative, an organization made up of current and former ICBM community members and their families that pushes the government to address higher rates of cancer and other illnesses among ICBM airmen, called the swift removal of those units “a great start.” But more work remains to be done, the organization said on social media.
“We need to create a culture where Airmen recognize hazards, speak up, and leaders respond—making the mission safer for those serving today and tomorrow,” Torchlight said in a post on LinkedIn.
Torchlight Initiative public affairs director Erin Dick said in an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine that while it was encouraging the Airman in this situation knew enough to recognize the potential PCB exposure and say something, it is concerning to think of how many Airmen may have used such contaminated equipment over the decades before PCB hazards were fully known.
Dick said the Air Force should work to determine how widespread potential exposures were, identify and document anyone who may have been exposed, and make sure their health is monitored over the long term, potentially including screenings.
The Air Force said in its release that the Airman in this incident returned to duty “with no adverse effects.” But Dick said it could be too soon to make that conclusion.
“It’s really not possible to say, because of the way these chemicals work, if there will be long-term health effects for this particular Airman,” Dick said. “There is often a very long latency period before illnesses appear. But at least now he’s got [PCB exposure] documented, and that is something we’re trying to encourage all people who are currently serving [and those who previously served] in the community to make sure that their service is documented.”
Retired Air Force Col. Jennifer Reeves, a former commander of the 341st Missile Wing at Malmstrom Air Force Base, Mont., told Air & Space Forces Magazine the recent discovery of PCBs underscores how important it is for the Air Force to remain vigilant against these kind of contaminants.
As part of the Missile Community Cancer Study, the Air Force in 2023 took air and swipe samples from all three of its active ICBM bases: Malmstrom, F.E. Warren, and Minot Air Force Base, N.D. The swipe tests involve gauze wetted with a solution run over surfaces and then analyzed for suspected contaminants. The tests showed a few samples with elevated PCB levels at Minot and Malmstrom, while F.E. Warren had trace amounts not in excess of the EPA’s acceptable limit.
“Typically the command has been actually pretty good, once [PCBs have] been found, about dealing with them,” Reeves, now a senior resident fellow for space studies at AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, said. “It’s really old stuff from back when we really weren’t tracking major chemicals and other things that are not good for humans. So now it’s about how well the command can react when things like this are found.”
Reeves said that because ICBMs still use many components from the years before PCBs were banned, the chemicals may still be out there in facilities. It’s crucial for the Air Force to keep looking for PCBs, she said, and the service needs to keep track and follow up with Airmen who may have come down with unusual conditions.
Air Force Global Strike Command also needs to come up with a way to go through its legacy equipment systematically and test them for PCBs, to make sure more potentially harmful gear isn’t out there, she said.
“The bigger context is not, ‘we found an isolated thing’” contaminated with PCBs, Reeves said. “This may be building a bigger picture that we may not yet be fully witting of.”

articles.title: The World Is Telling the Wrong Story About China
articles.body:
Compared with Donald Trump’s chaotic, divided, and violent America, China is a bastion of steady progress and serene order. This, at least, is the story that Beijing’s propagandists have been eager to spread. The Global Times, a Communist Party–run news outlet, proclaimed earlier this year that “the world’s peace and development increasingly rely on China’s stability.” The state news agency Xinhua chimed in that “in today’s uncertain world, China’s stability and predictability provide a rare and valuable anchor, which is set to benefit other countries.”
This message appears to be resonating around the world. A Pew Research Center survey of three dozen countries recently found that China is now seen more positively than the United States. Respondents expressed more confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping to “do the right thing” in world affairs than Trump.
China’s stability may appear desirable to a world in turmoil. But inside China, this “stability” looks a lot like policy paralysis, economic stagnation, and intensified political repression. What all the hand-wringing over China’s growing influence and surging exports fails to recognize is that the country is flatlining politically and economically. The evidence is in plain sight.
Policy makers around the world are understandably fixating on China’s abundant and cheap electric cars and competitive AI models, which present a serious threat to national industries. But these advances are one small part of a broader economy with pernicious and deep-rooted problems. The country’s property-market downturn, triggered by the 2021 meltdown of the real-estate developer Evergrande, has not hit bottom. Home prices continue to fall, eating away at the wealth of many middle-class households.
Trump’s war with Iran has pushed up oil prices, raising the cost of production for Chinese companies and ending three years of deflation. But the underlying problems of oversupply and weak demand remain entrenched. Youth unemployment, which emerged as a major social issue in 2023, has become chronic. The jobless rate among workers aged 16 to 24 stood at 18 percent last month.
These pressures have left Chinese consumers reluctant to spend. Retail sales grew a paltry 0.6 percent in July. Domestic sales of EVs have been falling. China’s economic problems have become so dire that some economists suspect that the official government statistics are overstating the country’s true performance. Although China’s economy has been growing a respectable 5 percent annually for the past three years, the research firm Rhodium Group estimates that China’s actual growth rate was probably near 2 percent in 2023 and closer to 3 percent over the past two years.
Any hope that China’s leaders will tackle these problems is almost certainly misplaced. Xi has stubbornly resisted the difficult and politically sensitive reforms necessary to fix the country’s economic model during his nearly 14 years in charge, and he is unlikely to change his approach anytime soon. He remains as myopically focused as ever on state-led programs to advance Chinese technology and industry, and particularly AI, and is apparently convinced that they will boost the entire economy. Perhaps this strategy will one day pay off, but the signs aren’t good. China’s debt has exploded on Xi’s watch—at three times the size of the economy, it surpasses even America’s debt burden. Growth in the second quarter of 2026 was the slowest since 2022, when China was still battling the coronavirus pandemic.
The Communist Party could theoretically change its leadership team at a major congress next year, but in the absence of any clear alternatives or successors, Xi is likely to secure yet another five-year term as general secretary. Xi’s ruthlessness in office has been marked by regular purges of possible rivals, generals, and members of other party factions. His latest victim appears to be Fang Xinghai, a former top securities regulator well-respected by international business leaders, against whom the party recently launched an investigation for unnamed disciplinary violations. With Fang’s fall, the government is sidelining yet another economic reformer with valuable expertise who might have helped fix the economy’s woes but whose market-oriented philosophy has fallen out of favor with a regime that prefers a top-down approach to national development.
Xi maintains social order through this never-ending malaise by controlling information and repressing alternative views. A sweeping new law took effect last month that mandates Mandarin as the primary language in education and orders parents to guide children to “love the Chinese Communist Party.” In prizing national unity over ethnic autonomy, this policy seems designed to force the country’s various ethnic minorities, including Uyghurs, Tibetans, and Mongolians, to assimilate into the majority Han Chinese culture. Even humor must follow the party line. Local authorities are reportedly investigating Guo Degang, a popular comedian who made the mistake of altering the lyrics of a patriotic song cherished by Communist cadres during a performance in the city of Wuhan last month.
Despite global surveys that report a growing fondness for China, the country’s “stability” comes at a steep cost to other countries. China may not be dropping bombs, but Beijing is arguably helping other countries drop theirs. By economically supporting Iran and Russia, Xi is essentially fighting proxy wars in both Europe and the Middle East.
In the absence of domestic demand, China’s subsidized and bloated manufacturing industries are exporting their problems and threatening the survival of competitors around the world. Given weak sales at home, Chinese automakers are shipping twice as much of their production overseas as they had a year ago. European Union officials are seeking greater powers and enhanced cooperation among its members to protect the continent’s industries from an onslaught of cheap Chinese imports, which have not only cost the region jobs but have run up a trade deficit with China topping $1 billion a day.
As Trump’s unpredictable and self-obsessed decision making saps America’s economic competitiveness and military might, China’s rise on the world stage is destined to continue, if only by default. But Xi’s insistence on preserving stability instead of addressing China’s serious structural problems threatens this ascent. Perhaps, then, the competition between China and the U.S. is less a contest for supremacy than a race to see which country hits bottom first.

articles.title: ‘Every step towards disarmament matters,’ nuclear testing survivors warn
articles.body:
‘Every step towards disarmament matters,’ nuclear testing survivors warn
He was born without arms, a legacy of four decades of nuclear explosions at the Semipalatinsk test site in his native Kazakhstan.
Artist and anti-nuclear activist Karipbek Kuyukov walked through the halls of UN Headquarters in New York on Monday alongside diplomats, scientists and survivors, carrying a message he has spent his life delivering: no one should ever again suffer what his generation endured.
Mr. Kuyukov, who paints holding the brush with his lips and toes, was among the participants of a symbolic walk ahead of the General Assembly’s high-level meeting on the occasion of the International Day against Nuclear Tests, marked annually on 29 August.
The short procession, part of the #StepUp4Disarmament campaign, ended in front of a large photograph on display in the General Assembly building, depicting people demanding the closure of the Semipalatinsk site.
“I would like to tell our story, the story of Kazakhstan,” Mr. Kuyukov told UN News.
456 nuclear tests
Between 1949 and 1989, the Semipalatinsk site saw 456 nuclear tests. Hundreds of thousands of people living nearby were exposed to elevated levels of radiation, with consequences carried within families across generations.
“My parents were living witnesses of those tests, and as a result, I was born without arms,” Mr. Kuyukov said.
He was 20 years old when Kazakh poet Olzhas Suleimenov launched the Nevada-Semipalatinsk anti-nuclear movement.
‘Entire nation rose up’
“The entire nation rose up against this monster, against the Semipalatinsk polygon,” he recalled.
The movement reached far beyond Kazakhstan.
Mr. Kuyukov remembered standing at a protest alongside a chief of the Shoshone people, whose lands lay near the United States test site in Nevada, and joining peaceful rallies at the gates of Semipalatinsk with activists from French Polynesia, where France conducted tests at Mururoa Atoll, and from Japan.
Shuttered for good
On 29 August 1991, the Semipalatinsk site was shut down, a date the General Assembly later proclaimed, at Kazakhstan’s initiative, as the International Day against Nuclear Tests. This year marks 35 years since the closure.
“I can say with pride that my country, Kazakhstan, began its path to sovereignty precisely with that peaceful decision,” Mr. Kuyukov said. “I believe this is a great honour for us and can serve as a worthy example for other countries.”
Every step counts
Addressing participants of the walk, UN High Representative for Disarmament Affairs Izumi Nakamitsu said the silence that fell upon Semipalatinsk 35 years ago “did not happen by chance”.
“It was achieved through the determination of people, communities and leaders who rejected nuclear testing,” she said.
Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to the UN Kairat Umarov described the walk as “a very simple but very powerful way to remind us that every step towards disarmament matters”.
This year also marks the 30th anniversary of the opening for signature of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT). Robert Floyd, Executive Secretary of the CTBT Organization, told the young people taking part in the walk that disarmament is “a journey that works across generations”.
“The day will come when your generation will lead, will make the decisions, will be in the boardrooms, will be in the assembly halls,” he said. “And we will be cheering on your great steps forward.”
No one immune
Speaking later in the General Assembly, Ms. Nakamitsu warned that concerns about a possible resumption of nuclear explosive testing have re-emerged amid deep geopolitical tension.
She recalled the Secretary-General’s message: “the world must never witness another nuclear explosion.”
The President of the General Assembly, Annalena Baerbock, stressed that the consequences of nuclear explosions know no borders.
“In an interconnected world such as ours, there is no truly ‘remote region’ immune from the effects or dangers of nuclear testing,” she said.
Five generations of cancer
Among the speakers was Tina Cordova, a fourth-generation survivor of the 1945 Trinity test in New Mexico, who also joined the morning’s symbolic walk.
“We were the first people exposed to radiation anyplace in the world as ash fell from the sky in the days after the bomb,” she told the Assembly, describing five generations of cancer in her family. “We were never warned before or after of the danger, so we lived our lives off the land as we always did.”
She closed with an appeal to the delegates, saying that “after 81 years, it is time we set our families, our children and grandchildren free from nuclear threat.”
Message to the young
For Mr. Kuyukov, the fight is now about those who come next. Seeing young people join movements against nuclear weapons always reminds him that “in war, it is innocent children who suffer first.”
“The future is in their hands,” he said. “They, too, must secure a safe world for the next generation. We have experience and we can share it because we know how this is done.”
Asked what he would say to world leaders at a time when, in his words, the situation in the world has become dangerously tense, the artist called for reconciliation.
“To reach a new world – one of kindness, mercy and compassion – we need to let go of old grievances and past mistakes and leave them in history,” he stressed. “Now, we can only move forward together, showing the way to the new generation.”

articles.title: NATO's Arctic moves pose 'direct threat' to Russia, foreign minister Lavrov says
articles.body:
NATO's Arctic moves pose 'direct threat' to Russia, foreign minister Lavrov says
Aug 31 - Russia sees NATO activity in the Arctic as a direct security threat, Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said in an article published on Monday, as the alliance members boost their presence in the region in the wake of Russia's war on Ukraine.
In February, NATO launched a mission called Arctic Sentry to bolster its presence in the far north, underscoring the alliance's increased focus on the Arctic amid tensions with Russia and U.S. President Donald Trump's push for the acquisition of Greenland.
Russia, which has a naval fleet including nuclear-armed submarines in the Arctic, sees the region as its sphere of interest where it also develops a shipping route to connect with the Asian nations.
Moscow has earlier protested the Arctic Sentry mission and in the article, Lavrov, President Vladimir Putin's long standing foreign minister, said Russia sees NATO military exercises in the region as 'aggressive'.
"Such military activity in the Far North poses direct threats to Russia's security. The risks of incidents that could trigger an armed confrontation, with potentially catastrophic consequences, are increasing," he said in the article published by the Russian foreign ministry.
Russia has the largest military presence and the most extensive military infrastructure in the Arctic and in recent years China has started to increase its activity in the mineral-rich area, mostly in partnership with Moscow.
Norway, a Russia's neighbour, this month expanded a recently created military brigade headquartered in the Arctic, the latest move by a NATO nation to boost its defence footprint in the wake of the Ukraine war which Russia started in 2022.
Moscow has previously dismissed allegations that it poses a threat to NATO. REUTERS

articles.title: Missile attack on Russia's Belgorod kills two, authorities say; hits Ozon facilities
articles.body:
Missile attack on Russia's Belgorod kills two, authorities say; hits Ozon facilities
Aug 31 - A missile attack killed two people and injured 16 in the city of Belgorod close to the Russian border with Ukraine, acting governor Alexander Shuvayev said on the Telegram messaging app.
Sunday's deaths followed Ukraine's hit on a commercial facility, which also set ablaze seven warehouses in the city, he added.
Russian online retailer Ozon said on Telegram that a logistics hub and a sorting facility in Belgorod also came under attack, triggering a fire and injuring people.
It was not immediately clear whether Shuvayev and Ozon were referring to the same facilities.
At least 38 were killed on Friday after a Russian drone attack sparked a detonation in an ammunition depot in the area of Ukraine's capital of Kyiv.
Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022. The two regularly exchange attacks on each other's infrastructure, including ports, energy and logistic facilities but deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Reuters could not independently confirm the damage reports.
Russia's top lender, Sberbank, has approved the restructuring of a total of 6.8 billion roubles ($79 million) in loans for traders of goods via Ozon and Wildberries, another e-commerce giant that recently drew Ukraine attacks, state news agency TASS said, citing a bank executive. REUTERS

articles.title: Iran warns any hostile act will be met with decisive response
articles.body:
“If the enemies make a mistake, their snouts will definitely be rubbed in the dirt,” said Brigadier General Alireza Elhami, who leads Iran’s Joint Headquarters of Air Defense, on Monday, according to Press TV.
His remarks were published hours after the United States carried out unprovoked attacks on Iranian military positions in the southern island of Larak.
Iran quickly responded by targeting US assets in the region.
The trading of fire came more than a month after the US attacked areas along the Iranian southern coast, while Iran responded by conducting extensive missile and drone operations targeting US bases in the region.
Elhami said the Iranian air defense force had unveiled several new interception systems over the past few days.
He said the new homegrown weapons have been manufactured relying on experience Iran gained during the US-Israeli aggression on the country that ended in a ceasefire in mid-April.
The commander said the unveilings carry an important message for Iran’s enemies.
Elhami said, however, that Iran has a policy to keep the details and information about its home-made weapons confidential.
“…by keeping this information confidential, we can make better use of them on the scene,” said Elhami, accoridng to Press TV.
The general said the new systems are only aimed at Iran’s enemies, and that the country maintains friendly and peaceful relations with its neighbors and countries in the region.
MNA

articles.title: Algeria Deploys Four Su-30 Fighter Jets to Republic of Niger Following Coup Attempt
articles.body:
Algeria has deployed four Su-30 fighter jets and an Il-78 aerial refueling tanker to Niger to support the country’s armed forces following an attempted military coup in the capital, Niamey.
This was reported by the Algerian Ministry of National Defence.
The decision was made following a request for assistance from the Nigerien authorities. The Algerian aircraft arrived at Diori Hamani International Airport in Niamey on the morning of August 30.
The Algerian military said it had deployed two patrol groups comprising four Su-30 fighter jets to support the Nigerien army and counter the attempted destabilization of the country.
The aircraft were accompanied by an Il-78 aerial tanker, which provides in-flight refueling for the fighter jets.
NEW: Algeria deployed four Su-30MKA fighter jets and an Il-78 tanker to Niger today after an attempted mutiny in Niamey.
The mission, requested by Nigerien authorities, was presented as a show of military support and appears to mark Algeria’s first known overseas Su-30… pic.twitter.com/iIJVwEsVJg
— Clash Report (@clashreport) August 30, 2026
Before landing in Niamey, the fighter jets conducted a flyover of the capital. Nigerien Prime Minister Ali Mahamane Lamine Zeine personally met the crews and thanked Algeria for its military support.
This marks a notable overseas deployment of Su-30 fighter jets for Algeria. It is the first known instance of Algerian fighters of this type being relocated to another country.
At the same time, Algeria’s official statement does not characterize the operation as a combat use of aircraft and contains no information about them carrying out strike missions.
The redeployment of the fighter jets came amid an attempted coup that began on August 29. A group of soldiers attacked key sites in Niamey, including Base 101 at the international airport and areas near the presidential palace.
Gunfire and explosions continued in the capital for several hours.
According to available information, military units from the country’s southwestern regions of Ouallam, Téra, and Dosso were involved in the assault.
Units from these regions have suffered significant losses over an extended period in fighting against a local branch of the Islamic State terrorist organization.
Despite the military leadership’s promises to stabilize the security situation, the country continues to suffer attacks by groups affiliated with Al-Qaeda and the Islamic State.

articles.title: Iran strikes two US airbases in Jordan
articles.body:
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it struck two U.S. airbases in Jordan — King Hussein and al-Azraq — with ballistic missiles on Monday, destroying technical and repair infrastructure and fighter aircraft positions.
In a statement, the IRGC said its aerospace forces carried out a combined missile and drone operation in response to an air attack by the "American-Zionist enemy" on the island of Larak. The operation targeted the technical and maintenance infrastructure and aircraft deployment areas at the two bases, inflicting heavy damage.
The IRGC warned that "aggression and crime" would not solve the enemy's failure to weaken Iran's control over the Strait of Hormuz, and that every strike would be met with "more crushing responses."

articles.title: It's time to move from endless war to end of war: PM to Putin
articles.body:
"Time to move away from endless war to end of war": PM Modi tells Russian Prez Putin on sidelines of SCO summit
With no end in sight to the Russia-Ukraine war, PM Narendra Modi renewed his message of peace to Russian President Vladimir Putin on Monday, saying on this occasion that it was time to move from an endless war to the end of war for the sake of humanity.Modi delivered the message in his opening remarks before a bilateral meet with Putin on the margins of the SCO heads of state summit in Bishkek in which the two focused on expanding cooperation in energy, defence, innovation, space, fertilisers and people-to-people linkages. The 'endless war to end of war' message is the latest in a series of televised statements made by Modi before Putin for the return of peace, beginning with his assertion in 2022- frequently cited by the Western world, one which even made it to the Bali Declaration - that this wasn't the era of war.That message too was delivered on the margins of an SCO summit in Samarkand. He followed it up with a message to Putin in Moscow in 2024 - in the midst of outrage in the West over his Russia visit - that no solution can be found on the battlefield.India's balancing act on the war saw Modi travelling to Ukraine a few months after his visit to Russia in 2024.Modi told Putin in Bishkek that India supports all efforts for peace and will continue to do so in future.
“Every day spent on the war pushes humanity back. And every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm. We will have to move from an endless war to an end of war, which is very important for humanity’s well-being,” said the PM.“That all issues are resolved peacefully as soon as possible is the call of humanity. This is the message of India. This is the message of the land of Gandhi and the land of Buddha — the path to peace,” said Modi, adding that he was looking forward to welcoming Putin for the Brics summit.According to foreign secretary Vikram Misri, PM Modi conveyed to Putin India’s readiness to do whatever is feasible and necessary to move the conflict towards an end because “it is exacting a very heavy toll on the global community at large”.“Had extensive discussions with President Putin. Discussed the full range of the India-Russia Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership. It is gladdening to see significant progress across various sectors in recent years,” Modi said on X.In his own televised statement, Putin acknowledged Modi’s personal attention to the development of bilateral ties. Putin said Russia was preparing “seriously” for the Brics summit in India.Putin also said Russia was preparing “seriously” for the Brics summit in India and highlighted that over the past 10 years, the number of Indian students in Russia has risen to 40,000.
According to an Indian readout, Modi and Putin exchanged views on India-Russia engagement in the multilateral arena, in particular at Brics under India’s chairship for 2026.“They also shared perspectives on key regional and global issues of mutual interest, including the conflicts in West Asia and the Black Sea region which have impacted maritime trade and the safety and security of Indian seafarers,” said the Indian readout, adding that Modi reiterated that dialogue and diplomacy were the way forward in resolving conflicts.Both Modi and Putin agreed to remain in touch to further strengthen the partnership, acknowledging its growth and resilience against the backdrop of geopolitical uncertainties.

articles.title: 'Move from endless war to end of war': PM Modi tells Putin; key details from Bishkek talks
articles.body:
'Move from endless war to end of war': PM Modi tells Putin; key details from Bishkek talks

PM Modi and Vladimir Putin hug during their bilateral meeting in Bishkek
NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Monday met Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, where the two leaders discussed bilateral ties and key global developments."Had extensive discussions with President Putin. Discussed the full range of the India-Russia Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership. It is gladdening to see significant progress across various sectors in recent years. Focus areas for the India-Russia friendship remain energy, innovation, space, fertilisers and people-to-people linkages," PM Modi said in a post on X.
'Move from endless war to end of war'
Prime Minister Narendra Modi called for an end to prolonged conflicts, saying that every day spent in war pushes humanity backwards, while steps towards peace bring renewed hope."Every day spent in war sets humanity back, whereas every step taken towards peace fills humanity with new hope and enthusiasm. We must move away from endless war and an end to the war. This is essential for the well-being of humanity," PM Modi said during his bilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Bishkek.Referring to the Ukraine conflict, PM Modi said India had consistently discussed the issue with Putin and remained committed to supporting peace efforts.
"We have consistently discussed the issue of Ukraine. When we met previously, you briefed me in detail on all aspects of the matter. As you know, India supports all efforts towards peace and will continue to do so," he said.Calling for an early peaceful settlement, PM Modi said, "A peaceful resolution to all issues at the earliest is the call of humanity, and this is India's message. The land of Gandhi and the land of Buddha share a single message- the path of peace. Today, I look forward to discussing these matters with you," he added.
PM Modi invites Putin for Brics Summit
PM Modi invited Putin to New Delhi for the upcoming Brics Summit in September."We are eager to welcome you to India for the Brics Summit in New Delhi this September," PM Modi said, adding that Putin's visit would "further strengthen India-Russia relations."Putin is scheduled to travel to New Delhi later this year for the summit.Putin thanked PM Modi for his role in maintaining India-Russia relations. "I'm very grateful to you for your personal attention to the Russia-India relationship," the Russian president said.The two leaders reviewed cooperation across areas of the bilateral partnership and exchanged views on pressing international issues.
PM Modi and Putin take car ride
Following their bilateral meeting, PM Modi and Putin travelled together in the same car to the opening ceremony of the VI World Nomad Games at Bishkek Arena.The meeting comes months after the last India-Russia Annual Summit, held in New Delhi during Putin's state visit on December 4-5, 2025. During that summit, the two countries adopted a joint statement and announced 21 outcomes, including 16 MoUs and agreements covering areas such as mobility, fertilisers, health, food safety, maritime cooperation, customs, commerce, academics and media.India and Russia have held 23 annual summits so far, alternately in the two countries. Their relationship was elevated to a "Special and Privileged Strategic Partnership" in 2010.Earlier, PM Modi met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, with the two leaders discussing the ongoing conflict in West Asia. It was their first bilateral meeting since the Iran-US conflict broke out in February."Calling for safeguarding the freedom of navigation and commerce, he (PM Modi) emphasised that civilians and civilian infrastructure, including commercial shipping and seafarers must not be harmed under any circumstances," MEA said.
During the meeting, PM Modi reiterated India's support for efforts to end the conflict and stressed the importance of freedom of navigation and protecting civilians and civil infrastructure in the region. "Met President Masoud Pezeshkian in Bishkek. Reiterated our commitment to strengthening India’s long standing friendship with Iran across diverse sectors," PM Modi said on social media.
"We want to expand and diversify our trade basket in the times to come. We had a discussion on the prevailing situation in the region. India will continue to support all efforts aimed at ensuring lasting peace," he said.
Aastha Jha is a writer at The Times of India, covering politics. She also writes on business, global affairs, social issues, with a focus on policy, governance and their impact on everyday lives. Her work brings together reportage and analysis, tracking developments in India and abroad while examining the broader social and economic currents shaping public discourse.

articles.title: Dual defence betrayal: China reveals rare case of executive spying for 2 countries
articles.body:
Dual defence betrayal: China reveals rare case of executive spying for 2 countries
Highly regarded employee who handled international business for Chinese military trading firm arrested for leaking sensitive information
An executive at a Chinese military trading company has been arrested for leaking sensitive defence information to intelligence agencies from two countries, Beijing’s top spy and anti-espionage agency revealed on Monday.
Public disclosures involving a Chinese national recruited simultaneously by multiple separate foreign intelligence agencies are extremely rare.
The ministry outlined the case of the suspect, identified only by his surname Zhang, in an article published on an official social media account.
The report did not name the two foreign countries involved, referring to them only as “Country A” and “Country B”. It also did not provide the name of the Chinese company or an exact timeline for the case.
According to the ministry, Zhang was fluent in an unknown number of foreign languages after spending years studying abroad. He returned to China and was highly regarded by his employer, frequently handling international business for the arms-trading firm.

articles.title: Ukrainian Defense Forces Strike Launcher and UAV Depot at Russia’s Tsimbulova Drone Base
articles.body:
In the early hours of August 30, the Ukrainian Defense Forces carried out a series of strikes on storage and launch facilities for Russian military attack UAVs at the Tsimbulova drone base.
Satellite imagery showing the aftermath of the attack was published by the monitoring communities Exilenova+ and Supernova+.
In particular, one of the launchers for Geran UAVs was hit at the drone base.
In addition to the launch position, a storage facility for attack UAVs was also hit, with signs of fire visible at the site.
The facility is located near the eponymous village in Russia’s Znamensky district of the Oryol region.
The site is located approximately 175–180 km from the Ukrainian border.
Between July and August, Russian forces completed the construction and deployment of 16 launchers for jet-powered UAVs at the Tsimbulova drone base.
The base’s infrastructure was expanded with 10 launchers for Geran-5 jet-powered UAVs and six launchers for Geran-4 UAVs.
Additionally, four launchers for Geran-3 UAVs and three launchers for standard Geran-2 drones have been installed at the site.
Satellite imagery has also revealed the construction of a large-scale anti-drone defense system around Russia’s Geran strike drone production facility in Alabuga Special Economic Zone.
The imagery shows dozens of large lattice towers appearing around the UAV production facilities and other buildings involved in supporting production.
The defense system consists of two rings of towers: an inner perimeter of shorter towers surrounding the key production facilities, and an outer perimeter of taller towers covering a much larger area.
