articles.title: Taiwan tracks 10 Chinese ships, 4 military aircraft
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked four Chinese military aircraft, six naval vessels, and four official ships around Taiwan between 6 a.m. on Sunday and 6 a.m. on Monday.
Three of the four People’s Liberation Army aircraft crossed the Taiwan Strait median line in the country’s northern air defense identification zone, according to the MND.
So far this month, Taiwan has tracked Chinese military aircraft 171 times and ships 387 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around Taiwan.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

articles.title: Russia’s Finance Ministry “forgot” about Ukraine while discussing the G20 meeting, although the US said Trump’s plan was discussed
articles.body:
Russia’s Finance Ministry “forgot” about Ukraine while discussing the G20 meeting, although the US said Trump’s plan was discussed
Kyiv • UNN
Russia’s Finance Ministry did not mention Ukraine in its G20 report. The US said that Bessent and Siluanov discussed Trump’s plan to end the war.
The Russian Ministry of Finance published its version of the talks during the meeting of G20 finance ministers and central bank governors in the United States, making no mention of discussions on ending the war against Ukraine. At the same time, US media and American officials reported that US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent discussed Donald Trump’s plan for settling the Russian-Ukrainian war with Russian Minister Anton Siluanov, reports UNN.
Details
The Russian Finance Ministry said that on the first day of the meeting, Siluanov participated in sessions on the global economic situation, stimulating economic growth, and resolving sovereign debt. The Russian ministry’s statement made no mention of Ukraine or talks on ending the war.
Siluanov, for his part, said it was necessary to restore the G20’s role as a financial coordination mechanism and identified “geopolitical fragmentation” and rising global debt as the main problems facing the global economy.
The US reported a completely different subject of the talks
Earlier, US media, citing representatives of the US administration, reported that Bessent held a separate meeting with Siluanov on the sidelines of the G20 in Asheville. According to CNBC, Fox Business, and other American media outlets, one of the topics was the plan proposed by the Trump administration to end the Russian-Ukrainian war.
A US official also confirmed to AFP that a possible settlement of the war was discussed during the meeting. At the same time, when reporting on Siluanov’s contacts in the United States, the Russian side limited itself to references to financial and economic issues.
During the G20, Siluanov himself said that automation, the introduction of artificial intelligence, import substitution, and other domestic factors had become new “growth points” for the Russian economy.
The report provided by the Russian Finance Ministry made no mention of talks with the American side regarding Ukraine.

articles.title: What to Watch from Trump’s US Space Academy Commission
articles.body:
President Donald Trump on Aug. 28 announced plans to establish a U.S. Space Academy to bolster the country’s workforce and educate “the next generation” of space experts.
The announcement quickly drew comparisons to existing military academies—in a speech at NASA’s Lyndon B. Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, Trump himself likened it to the Army’s United States Military Academy at West Point. But the White House executive order issued in conjunction with the president’s announcement indicates the vision is for a new kind of federal service academy, one led by NASA and designed to train space operators and engineers across the civil, military, and commercial sectors.
“To continue to lead the world in space exploration and technology, while securing and defending our national interests in space, the Nation must prepare the next generation of astronauts, scientists, engineers, operators, entrepreneurs, civil servants, and warfighters and ensure that they are capable of advancing American interests in space,” the order states. “It is my administration’s policy to strengthen the nation’s space workforce by expanding opportunities to educate and develop the next generation of leaders across the space domain.”
The President doesn’t have the authority to create the academy on his own—that would require an act of Congress—but his order establishes a commission to explore questions around the academy’s structure, potential military or civil service requirements, location, funding, and eligibility requirements. The group will be led by NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, and other commissioners will include leaders from the White House and the Pentagon, including the Secretary of Defense and the Secretary of the Air Force. The commission is meant to issue a report with recommendations by late December.
As those recommendations take shape in the coming weeks and months, experts say they’ll be watching for more detail on the academy’s mission and scope as well as efforts to garner feedback from members of Congress. They’ll also be tracking the U.S. military’s role in the organization and how it might impact the U.S. Air Force Academy, whose 2026 class included 93 Guardians. A Department of the Air Force spokesperson declined to comment for this story. In a statement, USAFA’s Association and Foundation, its alumni organization, said it will “closely monitor developments” and share relevant information with graduates.
Charles Galbreath, director of the Mitchell Institute’s Spacepower Advantage Center of Excellence, said the concept of a NASA-led “space center of excellence” makes sense given NASA’s deep knowledge and legacy operating in the domain.
“For decades, NASA has been the repository of knowledge when it comes to space operations,” Galbreath said. “It stands to reason that it would be useful to codify that, to create an academy where NASA experts could pass on that knowledge to the next generation.”
While the President’s order doesn’t specify the primary audience for the new academy, Galbreath said there’s an opportunity to reach a wide swath of the space community—from undergraduates to mid-career operators—with programming that ranges from certifications to academic degrees. For the military, the academy could eventually serve as a means for commissioning officers, but Galbreath said that may not be necessary immediately given the Space Force’s small size.
“At some point in the future, it could grow and become a commissioning source, I suppose,” he said. “But we’re still a long way from that.”
Todd Harrison, a space policy expert at the American Enterprise Institute, said that while he agrees there’s a need to expand the space workforce, it’s not clear that a new federally run academy is the right answer. In an interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine, he cited concerns about operational costs, blurring the line between military and civil space missions, and setting up unnecessary competition with the universities that already exist to train the aerospace workforce.
Harrison suggested that rather than create a separate academy, the administration could start a scholarship program similar to the Reserve Officers’ Training Corps, or ROTC. In this scenario, the government would offer scholarships to students pursuing relevant, space-related degrees in exchange for a period of service in the Space Force, NASA, or another federal agency.
“Instead of competing with our world-class institutions . . . you would let them produce the best and the brightest talent with a commitment to go into the government and work for the government for a period of time,” he said. “Establishing a physical academy is going to take years, whereas if you make it a scholarship program, you could literally start awarding scholarships next school year.”
While a scholarship program is one way to address the government’s workforce pipeline, Galbreath argued there’s also value in creating the consolidated hub of space expertise that would come with the academy model.
“When you have people that are colocated, they’re going to breed new ideas as well,” he said. “If you’re a student and you’re learning about orbital mechanics from a NASA PhD who designed the trajectories for a multi-planetary flyby, you’re getting the best.”
Another key question for the commission is where to locate the academy. Galbreath said it’s worth considering whether the academy should be located in a single campus or dispersed across multiple hubs, adding that cost will be an important factor as the commission considers its footprint.
Harrison cautioned that opening that discussion—which is often loaded with parochial politics—too soon could muddy the process. In fact, some lawmakers have already started to pitch their districts to house the Space Academy, including Rep. Dale Strong, R-Ala., who said on Aug. 31 that Huntsville, Ala., has been floated as a potential location. Although the commission has months to recommend a location, Trump indicated he may select one sooner.
Political headwinds may become a problem for Trump’s Space Academy proposal, especially if Republicans lose their majority in either the House or Senate after midterm elections in November. Harrison said there’s likely not enough time for the commission to complete its work and put the decision to a vote before the end of this legislative session.
But Galbreath noted that creating a new academy could garner bipartisan support, similar to the creation of the Space Force in 2019 during Trump’s first term.
“It’s really going to come down to the cost-benefit—can they make a compelling case that this Space Academy is going to be worth the investment of time and money and personnel,” he said. “If they can, then I think they’ll get bipartisan support. I don’t think this is one of those areas that you can get unilateral support.”
Some Democrats, including Rep. George Whitesides, D-Calif., have already indicated they’re intrigued by the concept. In an Aug. 28 post on the social media site X, Whitesides said the idea “deserves consideration” but raised concerns about funding and the lack of congressional representation on the commission.
“I am open-minded to hear thoughtful answers to these questions, but I recommend that Congress be engaged quickly and substantively or else this intriguing idea will be stuck on the launch pad,” Whitesides said.

articles.title: Israeli fire kills five people in Gaza, medics say
articles.body:
Israeli fire kills five people in Gaza, medics say
CAIRO, Aug 31 - Israeli airstrikes killed at least five Palestinians in the Gaza Strip on Monday, health officials said.
Medics said two people were killed and several others wounded when one strike hit a crowd near the municipal public park in Gaza City, an area packed with displaced families.
Later on Monday, another Israeli airstrike hit a vehicle in the Tel Al-Hawa neighbourhood in western Gaza City, killing at least three people, medics added.
The Israeli military said the two attacks targeted Hamas militants, without giving further information.
At Al Shifa Hospital, the enclave's largest medical facility, relatives and friends paid their last respects to two of the five men killed on Monday before carrying the white-shrouded bodies to the cemetery to bury them.
"There is no ceasefire. There is not one good day in Gaza since October 7 (2023)," said Amjad Abu Abdo, a relative of one of the people who died in the first strike on Monday.
"I swear, we do not sleep from the sound of drones. You sleep scared of being hit," Abu Abdo added.
Hamas-led fighters killed 1,200 people during their cross-border attack into Israel on October 7, 2023, according to Israeli tallies. The Gaza health ministry says Israeli attacks have killed more than 73,000 Palestinians in the enclave since then.
An October 2025 U.S.-backed ceasefire halted major fighting in the shattered territory, but it failed to end strikes by the Israeli military which says such actions are aimed at thwarting attacks by Hamas and other Gaza militants.
Hamas accuses Israel of violating the ceasefire and undermining efforts to implement a broader plan by U.S. President Donald Trump to end the Gaza conflict, which also includes Israeli withdrawals and Hamas disarmament.
More than 1,300 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the ceasefire took effect in October, according to Gazan health officials. The Israeli military says four Israeli soldiers have been killed. REUTERS

articles.title: Supreme Court lets Trump’s White House ballroom construction continue
articles.body:
Supreme Court lets Trump’s White House ballroom construction continue
- The US Supreme Court allowed Trump’s administration to continue building a $400 million White House ballroom despite legal challenges from a historic preservation group.
- The court’s 5-4 ruling, led by conservative justices, cited lack of legal standing by plaintiffs and national security risks if construction stopped.
- Chief Justice Roberts dissented, stating the project is likely unlawful without Congress’s approval, emphasising presidential limits on altering federal property.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The US Supreme Court in a 5-4 ruling on Aug 31 let Donald Trump’s administration continue construction of his White House ballroom complex while the president challenges a judicial order that would halt much of the development, with Chief Justice John Roberts in a dissent calling the project “likely unlawful.”
The court granted the administration’s request to block a Lower Court’s order halting above-ground construction of the US$400 million (S$508.49 million) ballroom while a lawsuit by a historic preservation group seeking to stop the project proceeds.
The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued in 2025 after the administration tore down the White House East Wing and began building a 90,000sq ft ballroom without seeking specific approval from Congress.
Trump has said the ballroom will be “the greatest of its kind ever built.”
The Aug 31 ruling, lauded by Trump, was powered by five of the court’s six conservative justices.
They wrote that the plaintiffs in the case, the non-profit National Trust for Historic Preservation, lacked the necessary legal standing to sue.
They also said the government would likely suffer “irreparable harm” if the project were blocked, citing national security concerns.
Roberts was the only conservative justice to dissent. He was joined in his dissent by the court’s three liberal justices.
The ballroom construction is “likely unlawful,” Roberts wrote, noting that Congress has “plenary constitutional authority over the District of Columbia and federal property” and that it has prohibited structures from being built on federal government grounds in Washington DC without its authorisation.
“The ballroom is a building or structure being erected on federal park grounds – President’s Park – in the District of Columbia. Yet Congress has not passed any law resembling ‘express authority’ for the Executive’s construction of it,” Roberts wrote.
The ‘golden age’
Trump in a social media post welcomed the ruling and called the legal challenge baseless.
“I am pleased to report that the United States Supreme Court has just ruled in favour of the Ballroom/Military Complex being built without any further contingency, doubt, or threat. We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington DC,” Trump wrote.
Roberts on Aug 21 had imposed a brief administrative stay to give the court additional time to consider the Trump administration’s request.
In an Aug 14 filing to the Supreme Court, Justice Department lawyers echoed the Republican president’s contention that the project is a security necessity, citing assassination attempts against the president and other recent threats.
“This case involves an extraordinary and unlawful injunction that will halt the ongoing construction of the integrated military complex, including a totally secure ballroom space, at the East Wing of the White House, which is vitally required by national security,” they wrote.
The project combines the above-ground ballroom with an extensive underground complex.
Trump has said the project includes bomb shelters, medical facilities, shielding from drones and missiles and other security features that are “all tied together as one big, expensive and very complex unit.”
On Aug 7, the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit in a 2-1 ruling upheld US District Judge Richard Leon’s order directing the administration to halt above-ground construction.
‘A temporary tenant’
“Each President is a temporary tenant, not the owner, of the White House,” and cannot fundamentally reshape it without congressional approval, the DC circuit’s ruling stated.
The district judge’s order did not permanently bar construction of a ballroom.
It blocked above-ground efforts while allowing below-ground construction to continue, as well as work deemed “strictly necessary” for the safety and security of the White House.
In its ruling, the DC circuit said national security arguments “are not an automatic get-out-of-law-free card.”
The Justice Department said in its Aug 14 filing that the overall East Wing project – including both the underground facilities and the above-ground ballroom – is 65 per cent complete.
Trump has said the ballroom project is a security necessity, and has referred to the structure as a “military centre” in a post on Truth Social.
Trump called the DC circuit’s decision “horrendous” and politically motivated, and said it left him, other White House officials and visitors exposed to attack.
“This unjust decision must be overturned by the Supreme Court in its entirety,” Trump wrote.
The National Trust for Historic Preservation in court papers urged the justices to turn away the administration’s bid to continue with ballroom construction while litigation proceeds.
“Each court to examine the question has agreed that (the Trump administration has) no unilateral legal authority – constitutional, statutory or otherwise – to build a massive ballroom on the site of the now-demolished East Wing,” lawyers for the group wrote.
“And each court has told (the administration) in no uncertain terms that they must stop their illegal construction unless and until they receive express approval from Congress,” it wrote.
The project is part of Trump’s broader efforts to reshape the Washington landscape, including plans to build a 76m arch and revamp the Kennedy Centre, a cultural landmark and performance centre.
The demolished East Wing housed the first lady’s offices and the White House movie theatre.
It was originally built in 1902 during Theodore Roosevelt’s presidency and greatly expanded in 1942 during Franklin Roosevelt’s presidency.
The Supreme Court, with its 6-3 conservative majority, has frequently ruled in favour of Trump in his second term in office, with some notable exceptions, as he has pushed to expand his powers in domestic affairs and foreign policy. REUTERS

articles.title: Russia Calls NATO Activity in Arctic a ‘Direct Threat’
articles.body:
Russia considers increased NATO military activity in the Arctic a direct threat to its security.
This was stated by Russian Minister of Foreign Affairs Sergey Lavrov.
Lavrov claims that NATO military exercises and other activities in the Arctic are ‘aggressive’ in nature.
According to him, such activity increases the risk of incidents that could lead to an armed confrontation.
“Such military activity in the Far North poses direct threats to Russia’s security,” Lavrov stated.
Lavrov’s statement came after NATO launched the Arctic Sentry mission in February 2026, aimed at strengthening the Alliance’s military presence in the Arctic.
NATO links its increased attention to the region to growing tensions in its relations with Russia.
The operation was launched in response to Russian activity in the region and increased intelligence efforts, both surface and underwater.
NATO believes Russia is directing its forces toward detecting and potentially damaging undersea infrastructure, particularly communications cables. Such actions could threaten communication links between the United Kingdom, Scandinavia, and other European countries.
At the same time, Russia and China are promoting the use of the Northern Sea Route as an alternative for international shipping amid instability around the Suez Canal and in the Middle East.
Moscow actively uses the development of Arctic routes for propaganda purposes, presenting them as a promising alternative to traditional shipping lanes. At the same time, Russia is strengthening its military presence in the region to ensure their operation.
Moscow says the deployment of military forces is necessary to ensure the safety of civilian shipping and protect Arctic infrastructure.
At the same time, Russian forces are actively conducting intelligence activities in the region, raising concerns among NATO countries.

articles.title: Crypto giant Tether promised careful vetting. Some early customers were later implicated in financial crimes.
articles.body:
CRYPTOCURRENCY
Crypto giant Tether promised careful vetting. Some early customers were later implicated in financial crimes.
Financial records obtained by ICIJ show that they included individuals later accused of or sanctioned for money laundering and other financial crimes.
During a two-month period in 2020, a Russian man named Nikita Krasnov purchased about $1.16 million worth of newly minted USDT — the widely used stablecoin made by the cryptocurrency company Tether. A little more than four years later, Krasnov was sanctioned by U.S. authorities for his role in an expansive sanctions evasion scheme catering to Russian elites.
It’s a story that repeats itself across Tether’s customer base. Tether’s USDT token, whose value is pegged 1-to-1 to the U.S. dollar, has become one of the most widely used types of cryptocurrency in illicit finance. But the 12-year-old company has long claimed that it does thorough due diligence on its primary customers — that is, the people and institutions who purchase USDT directly from Tether, rather than from secondary sources once the tokens are in general circulation. In a 2023 letter, Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino assured members of Congress that the company uses vetting practices that “you would see at sophisticated financial institutions,” such as reviewing customers’ sources of funds, sanctions lists and any other information that links them to illicit activity.
A set of Tether documents obtained by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists suggests otherwise. The documents show who was buying USDT tokens from Tether during 2019 and 2020 — a key period of growth for the company, when its tokens in circulation rose from less than $2 billion to more than $20 billion.
Although several years old, the records give a rare look into exactly who was buying USDT from Tether. Among them were some possibly concerning clients. These included hundreds of millions of dollars in purchases by shell companies based in the Cayman Islands, British Virgin Islands, the Seychelles and Hong Kong. More significantly, ICIJ identified several actors later revealed to be involved with financial crimes who together bought tens of millions of tokens directly from Tether. Among them were firms later named as laundering vehicles for North Korean hackers and for the Sinaloa Cartel, which smuggles vast amounts of heroin and fentanyl into the United States.
While Tether sold tokens to these customers years before their alleged crimes came to light publicly, the transactions raise questions about how closely Tether scrutinized the buyers. The purpose of thorough customer vetting goes beyond identifying known lawbreakers; its aim is also to understand customers’ sources of wealth and the nature of their business in order to detect fishy activity, especially when dealing in millions of dollars, according to experts.
“A lot of due diligence is to prevent you from onboarding a customer who later turns out to be a criminal,” Alison Jimenez, an anti-money laundering expert, told ICIJ. “You need to understand where the $50 million came from.”
In the documents examined by ICIJ, the identities of some of Tether’s customers are obscured behind shell companies in offshore tax havens known for secrecy. Others went on to become prominent players in crypto markets.
Perhaps the most infamous Tether customer is Alameda Research, which was co-founded by Sam Bankman-Fried, and was closely tied to Bankman-Fried’s FTX crypto exchange. Bankman-Fried is now serving a 25-year federal prison sentence for crimes related to his looting of more than $8 billion from FTX customer accounts. During the 17-month period recorded in the documents, Alameda Research — which served multiple, and sometimes conflicting roles, as a crypto hedge fund, a venture capital firm and a market-maker — purchased more than 4.1 billion USDT tokens directly from Tether.
As chronicled in other journalistic investigations and in Bankman-Fried’s own court trial, Alameda performed an essential role in buying billions of dollars’ worth of USDT from Tether and then putting them into wider circulation. A 2021 report on the website Protos named Alameda Research and a number of Tether’s other institutional customers.
The documents ICIJ obtained also list a group of previously-unknown buyers later linked to serious financial crimes. Tether directly did more than $100 million in deals with a pair of Hong Kong shell companies that a group of sanctions authorities from 11 countries say was used to access banking services and launder cryptocurrency proceeds for a notorious hacking and ransomware group run by North Korean intelligence operatives.
One of these companies, Lucky DC Trade Pty Limited, purchased nearly $47 million in USDT straight from Tether in 2020. Lucky DC’s director, Cheng Hung Man, was indicted by a federal grand jury in 2022 for laundering money for Pyongyang. The sanctions authorities said Cheng also used a firm called Tomorrow Good Limited to launder funds. That company purchased more than $66 million in USDT directly from Tether in 2019, according to the Tether sales document. It also appeared in a 2024 indictment of Sinaloa Cartel members that described how the Mexican drug gang laundered funds using USDT.
The documents also show that a Cayman Islands firm called AP Capital Investment Limited purchased $23.7 million in USDT directly from Tether in 2020. A few years later, it was cited in a Vietnamese case in which two men were sentenced to prison for an illicit trading scheme involving USDT, according to press reports from 2024.
“The case referred to solely concerns the conduct of certain local individuals,” Chris Humphries, a Cayman Islands attorney representing AP Capital Investment Limited told ICIJ. “The case is suspended with regard to the company due to insufficient evidence.”
Another early Tether customer, Ianis Antropenko, was indicted in 2024 on federal charges of targeting healthcare facilities and educational institutions with ransomware. Antropenko’s guilty plea earlier this year included an agreement to forfeit $1.4 million in USDT as well as other cryptocurrencies.
Krasnov, the Russian Tether customer who was sanctioned in 2024, played a key role in the criminal organization targeted in Operation Destabilise, the U.K. National Crime Agency’s largest anti-money laundering operation in a decade. The Economist magazine later pointed to the case in an article that called Tether’s stablecoin a “money launderer’s dream currency.” Krasnov’s direct purchase of tokens from Tether in 2020 has not been previously reported.
The Tether sales document does not include the wallet addresses — the crypto equivalent of a bank account number — that the firm’s customers used to receive the USDT they purchased. But ICIJ matched the dollar amounts and dates of dozens of the sales to specific transactions recorded in public blockchain data. The analysis shows that one of the wallet addresses Krasnov used to receive tokens from Tether was named by the U.S. Treasury Department in 2024 as a key money laundering account.
ICIJ also matched the transactions of two other Tether customers that the sales document lists as Russian nationals who together purchased more than $57 million tokens from Tether. These two customers used another wallet address that Krasnov used to receive USDT, although that wallet was not later sanctioned. The common address suggests those two customers were part of the same financial network as Krasnov, according to Paul Sibenik of Cryptoforensic Investigators, who reviewed the data at ICIJ’s request. Attempts to reach Krasnov were unsuccessful.
Tether says it subjects its direct customers to strict vetting. As for tokens that are acquired in general circulation by bad actors, Tether touts its work with law enforcement to freeze billions in illicit fund flows and its assistance in law enforcement investigations has become highly sought-after by agencies around.
“Tether has a long record of voluntarily assisting law enforcement agencies with investigations involving illicit activity,” the firm recently told ICIJ. Government investigators and crypto analysts who they work with have described Tether’s assistance in fast-moving crypto investigations as invaluable and say the company has been in some cases more responsive to law enforcement needs than other issuers of stablecoins.
Tether did not respond to requests to comment for this story.
Although Tether is supposed to hold one dollar in cash or cash equivalents, like U.S. Treasury bills, for each USDT token it mints, the company has been accused of issuing USDT without 1-to-1 dollar backing. In 2021, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission fined Tether $41 million for issuing misleading statements about its dollar reserves. New York’s attorney general also required Tether and Bitfinex, its affiliated crypto exchange, to pay $18.5 million in penalties for making false statements about Tether’s backing and ordered the firms to discontinue trading activity with New Yorkers.
Tether went on to buy billions of dollars’ worth of U.S. Treasuries with the help of Cantor Fitzgerald, the New York-based financial firm whose former chairman and CEO, Howard Lutnick, serves as President Trump’s commerce secretary. One of Lutnick’s sons, Brandon Lutnick, succeeded his father as chairman of Cantor Fitzgerald, which reportedly bought rights to a 5% interest in Tether, and has said that he personally verified Tether’s reserves.
As USDT surged to become a cornerstone of the crypto economy, Tether made deep inroads in politics, establishing its headquarters in bitcoin-friendly El Salvador and hiring former Trump crypto adviser Bo Hines.
One of the largest buyers of USDT in the records ICIJ reviewed is the eccentric Chinese entrepreneur Justin Sun, founder of the Tron blockchain, where about half of all USDT tokens now circulate. From April 2019 to March 2020, Sun purchased more than $214 million worth of USDT from Tether. Sun has had his hands in many pots, from advising the sanctioned crypto exchange HTX to participating in crypto projects at a Chinese school that trains future Communist Party leaders. During the Biden administration, the SEC accused Sun of selling unregistered securities and “fraudulently manipulating the secondary market for TRX,” his Tron token, which Lindsay Lohan, Jake Paul, and six other celebrities were allegedly quietly paid to promote alongside BTT, another Sun-affiliated token.
Later, Sun became one of the biggest buyers of the TRUMP memecoin and World Liberty Financial’s WLFI token. Earlier this year, the SEC resolved the case by dismissing its claims against Sun while one of his companies, Rainberry, agreed to pay a $10 million penalty. (Sun has since sued World Liberty Financial, claiming the Trump family crypto company stiffed him.)
Other Tether customers who appear in the documents obtained by ICIJ were later fined by U.S. regulators or arrested by foreign authorities. In 2023, Nexo Capital, a Cayman Islands-based crypto firm with more than $11 billion in assets under management, agreed to pay a total of $45 million in fines, divided equally between the SEC and regulators in multiple states.
A spokesperson for Nexo said that both “matters were concluded on agreed terms in 2023 and have been closed since” and that the regulatory actions had no bearing on the firm’s purchase of Tether tokens.
A company owned by Zhao Dong, a Chinese crypto trader and Bitfinex shareholder, received approximately $1.5 million worth of USDT over eight days in 2020. Chinese authorities later arrested him for suspected money laundering; he was convicted and spent several years in prison.
UKDE, which acquired roughly $867,000 worth of USDT, was the subject of a consumer warning from the U.K.’s financial regulatory authority in 2023 for providing unauthorized financial services. The company, which had raised at least $12 million in investment capital, has been liquidated, its phone number disconnected. If you go to its old website, ukde.com, you’ll be automatically forwarded to another site that reveals the fate of the former Tether client. It says: “This domain has been seized by the Bergen County Prosecutor’s Office, Financial Crimes Unit.”

articles.title: Breaking Through Infoglut: Australia’s Anger-information Overload Cycle
articles.body:
Why are we so angry? The easy, lazy, and entirely wrong explanation is that our technologies are to blame: the internet, smartphones, social media, artificial intelligence, and so on.
That’s the argument behind Australia’s doomed social media ban for young people, which is inspired by the deceptive claims and cherry-picked statistics peddled by pop-psychology influencers like Jonathan Haidt in his roundly debunked book “The Anxious Generation,” and driven by a moral panic that was cynically manufactured by the Murdoch media.
So why are we so anxious, and angry? Take the average 20-year-old in Australia: born into the aftermath of the 2008 Great Financial Crisis, they have seen companies reap record profits while for ordinary Australians the prospect of affordable housing has slipped ever further from their grasp.
They grew up in the shadows of the unresolved conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan and today encounter a daily dose of death and destruction in the reporting from Ukraine, Gaza, Iran, and other conflict hotspots. They spent their most formative teenage years in COVID lockdowns and Zoom schooling, while conspiracy theorists tried to convince their parents that the pandemic was a hoax perpetuated by some global cabal.
They’ve experienced more than a decade of the hottest years in human memory during their lifetime, most likely lived through one or more natural disasters in their area and yet have seen utter political inaction on the climate crisis. And those of us who are older have simply experienced all that for longer.
So how could they, and we, not be anxious and angry – regardless of whether we use smartphones and social media, or not? As David Weinberger wrote as early as 2004, in his fabulous take-down of the “echo chamber” fallacy, “the problem with an extraterrestrial-conspiracy mailing list isn’t that it’s an echo chamber,” facilitated by the digital platforms of the day: rather, the problem is “that it thinks there’s a conspiracy by extraterrestrials.”
The same goes for climate crisis denialists, anti-vaccination activists, sovereign citizens, far-right extremists, and other anti-social, anti-societal, and anti-democratic groups: it’s their angry, extreme, exclusionary, and uncompromising views that are the problem, rather than the technologies they use to express and spread them; if they didn’t have X as a platform that actively endorses their views, they’d find another.
Wherever that anxiety and anger comes from, whether “the internet” (whatever that means these days) or the other threatening scenarios: together they have highlighted the complex world we live in.
Conspiracy as Comfort
Let’s take one example: the observation that pandemics like COVID-19 simply happen from time to time and that there’s little more we can do than simply to prepare for the next one, is entirely correct, of course, but also deeply unsatisfying. It’s a great deal more convenient to comfort ourselves with fairytales of bioweapon factories, lab leaks, depopulation agendas, or interference by the Illuminati, aliens, or the Antichrist: they provide a concrete target for our anxiety, anger and action.
Where our modern communication technologies do come in is in the fact that they’ve made all that information – “real” as much as “fake” – so much easier to access and circulate, globally and instantly.
This substantially contributes to an information overload: we can readily access WHO reports about the pandemic and its causes, the more or less careful and insightful coverage of those reports by the world’s media, but also the “explainer” writings and videos of conspiracy theorists and influencers that cherry-pick and misrepresent those facts in order to perpetuate their “alternative” worldviews.
We’re overloaded by this infoglut: we, all of us, have neither the time nor the subject matter expertise to be able to reliably distinguish verified facts from made-up stories, or well-supported conclusions from far-fetched conjecture.
Ironically, the problem we are facing – the reason we are so angry – is the very opposite of the claims made by those still peddling the “echo chamber” and “filter bubble” fallacies that see us all in self-insulating bubbles: rather, the hyperconnectivity enabled by our current media environments produces an information overload that we are ill-equipped to process or reduce.
We may not consciously articulate this all the time, but deep down we recognize this, and that makes us anxious, and even angry. For many, the coping mechanism is to reach for easy explanations and ready-made scapegoats (elites, migrants, secret societies, other countries – or generally, others who simply are not like us).
But that story isn’t new; in fact, it is perhaps as old as humanity itself, even if it now plays out across a different media landscape.
It can’t be solved by banning smartphones, or social media, or AI; indeed, conspiracy theories and other disinformation usually only reach a broader audience when they’re also amplified by politicians, celebrities, and mainstream media.
Anxiety Fuels Scapegoating
Uncertainty produces rumors, which generate anxiety, which results in the scapegoating and exclusion of others; the commercial imperatives of mainstream media as well as social media encourage this further, as both seek sustained audience engagement.
Any attempts to deal with these destructive dynamics must focus first and foremost on the underlying causes of our anxiety and anger, of course; to return to where we started, as governments in Australia and elsewhere are beginning to find out, you don’t make young people less anxious by preventing them from communicating about their anxieties, but by paying serious attention to their actual concerns.
At the same time, we must confront the challenges of hyperconnectivity and information overload more directly, and central to this is to improve literacy in all its forms. This includes, of course, news and digital media literacy, to enable citizens better to distinguish quality, reliable information and sources from those that seek to mislead and enrage them; societal and civic literacy, to improve public understanding of the mechanisms of government and governance in Australia and elsewhere.
We must also ensure that citizens understand their individual rights and (just as importantly) obligations towards others within society, and enhance scientific literacy (across both social and natural sciences) to prevent them from falling prey to scientistic cherry-picking, whether on climate change or the effects of social media use.
Together those initiatives aim to save Australia from a trajectory that promotes deeply polarized, winner-takes-all politics as we see it played out in U.S. politics. Instead, they redirect citizens toward an understanding of political debate that is oriented toward workable compromise between legitimate diverging opinions, even if consensus remains unattainable.
To achieve that will not be a quick fix. It will be a generational project. However, Australia can learn from other countries here: from Finland’s successful media literacy strategy, and Germany’s Federal Agency for Civic Education.
Indeed, education at all levels, from primary to tertiary and beyond to lifelong learning, is central to this, and a substantial boost in investment will be required even just to avoid a further decline in media literacy levels across the population in the short term. All the more important that we confront this urgently, then: if we don’t, we’ll only grow more anxious and ever more angry.

articles.title: Russian literary monument returns to Dresden
articles.body:
Russian literary monument returns to Dresden
A monument to world-famous 19th-century Russian author Fyodor Dostoevsky has been reinstalled in the eastern German city of Dresden after spending around a year in storage. The ceremony was attended by Russian Ambassador to Germany Sergey Nechayev, who thanked the city authorities for their commitment to preserving cultural and humanitarian ties between the two nations.
Initially unveiled in 2006 during a ceremony attended by Russian President Vladimir Putin and then-German Chancellor Angela Merkel, the monument was installed on the bank of the Elbe River near the regional parliament building. In 2025, it was removed because of nearby construction work.
The city authorities then decided to move it to a new location, and the monument was reinstalled near the Russian Orthodox Church of St. Simeon of the Wonderful Mountain in the southern part of the city on Saturday.
The ambassador thanked Saxony’s regional government and the city authorities for bringing the monument back amid tense relations between Moscow and Berlin.
“I would particularly like to thank everyone who did not allow this story to end on a somber note and who persevered in ensuring that [the monument to] Dostoevsky could once again be where a monument belongs – in the public sphere,” Nechayev said, adding that “culture cannot and must not become a pawn in short-term political games.”
Cultural ties “should remain a bridge, a space for dialogue between societies, academic communities, cultural institutions, and individual citizens,” the diplomat added in a statement issued on the occasion. Saturday’s ceremony was attended by a group of Russian diplomats, as well as members of the German-Russian Institute of Culture in Dresden.
Russian culture faces pressure in the EU amid the continued hostilities between Moscow and Kiev. Since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, several EU member states have canceled events involving performers from Russia and other countries perceived as sympathetic to Moscow or barred Russian artists from participating.
Literature has not been spared in this anti-Russian drive either. In July, Latvia’s parliament approved a ban on Russian books and literature, among other consumer goods, claiming that Russia uses books and periodicals to spread propaganda and maintaining that the EU does not need such materials.
Kiev announced plans to take all Russian and Russian-language books out of circulation in Ukraine back in February. The Ukrainian authorities have steadily cracked down on the use of the Russian language in public life, restricting or banning its use in the media and in professional spheres. Imports of Russian and Belarusian books into Ukraine were banned as early as 2016.
Moscow has repeatedly denounced such measures as “Russophobic censorship,” warning that attempts to “cancel” Russian culture will ultimately fail.
Dostoevsky had a special connection with Dresden, where he lived with his family for some two years between 1869 and 1871 and spent an important period of his creative life working on the novel ‘Demons’. The author’s relationship with Germany was not always rosy, though. Dostoevsky developed a gambling addiction while living in the German spa town of Baden-Baden, which was known for its casinos at the time. In February 1867, he spent over four weeks playing roulette and lost everything, including his wife’s wedding ring. His constant lack of money also forced him to write one of his novels, ‘The Gambler’, in just 21 days.
Critics have also interpreted many of the author’s works, including the world-famous ‘Crime and Punishment’ and ‘The Brothers Karamazov’, as veiled criticism of classical German philosophy, including that of Hegel and Kant, as Dostoevsky rebelled against the idea of rationalizing individual suffering as a sufficient price for historical progress and universal “harmony.”

articles.title: Two Russian Pantsir-S1 SPAAGM Systems Destroyed in Crimea and Kuban
articles.body:
The Ukrainian Defense Forces destroyed two Russian Pantsir-S1 self-propelled anti-aircraft gun-missile systems in occupied Crimea and Russia’s Krasnodar Krai.
This was reported by the Telegram channel Dosye Shpiona, which published photos of destroyed equipment.
The first Pantsir-S1 SPAAGM system was destroyed on August 29 near the occupied city of Kerch in Crimea.
The second system was hit on August 30 near the military airfield in Yeysk, Krasnodar Krai.
According to the CyberBoroshno OSINT project, the Russians had also deployed a decoy near the system, but it did not protect the actual combat vehicle.
The Pantsir-S1 is a Russian short-range self-propelled system designed to protect civilian and military facilities from drones, cruise missiles, and aircraft.
The system is armed with two twin-barrel 2A38M 30 mm automatic cannons and 12 guided surface-to-air missiles. The cannons have an engagement range of up to 4 km, while the missiles can engage targets at ranges of up to 20 km and altitudes of up to 15 km.

The laptop, the social media user and the false alarm in Taiwan over a Beijing ‘spy’
Persistent fears of mainland infiltration risk raising unnecessary suspicion and eroding public trust, analysts say
A false espionage alarm about a Taipei subway user has fuelled concerns that growing fears of Beijing are breeding unhealthy suspicion on the island and eroding public trust.
The controversy erupted after a social media user posted a photograph of a man holding a laptop on a Taipei Main Station metro platform on Saturday.
Seeing the words “2nd Theatre Photosynthesis System” appeared in simplified Chinese on the laptop’s screen, the social media user suspected that the man was a mainland Chinese spy on a mission.
The social media user reported the man to several government agencies, including the police, immigration authorities, the Mainland Affairs Council and the Ministry of Justice’s Investigation Bureau.
She warned that if information about passenger flows, surrounding facilities and public movements at Taipei Main Station were collected and analysed by Beijing, it could potentially be used to plan wartime attacks or disrupt transport.

articles.title: Trump was sending message to Iran with Kharg Island post, says Vance
articles.body:
Trump was sending message to Iran with Kharg Island post, says Vance
- US President Trump used a social media post about Kharg Island to send a strategic message to Iran, according to Vice-President J.D. Vance.
- Trump’s post included an AI-generated video, but US officials confirmed no military strikes targeted Kharg Island overnight.
- Iranian officials dismissed the post as "laughable," while US forces reportedly attacked two Iranian launchers on Larak Island, marking the first strikes since late July.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - US President Donald Trump was sending a message to Iran with his social media post about Iran’s energy hub of Kharg Island being blown to smithereens, Vice-President J.D. Vance said on Aug 31.
“The president likes to switch it up on social media a little bit. He would be the first to say he doesn’t make announcements about military actions on social media, but I think that he’s sending a message to the Iranians,” Vance said when asked about Trump’s post.
Trump’s one-line social media post on Aug 30 was accompanied by an AI-generated video clip.
A US official said on Aug 31 the military had not targeted Kharg Island in overnight strikes.
An Iranian official dismissed Trump’s post as “laughable”.
Attacking Kharg, which handled 90 per cent of Iran’s oil exports before the war launched by US and Israeli attacks on Feb 28, would severely disrupt its energy trade and put huge pressure on its economy.
In describing the first known US military strikes since late July, a US official said forces attacked two Iranian launchers on Larak Island. REUTERS

articles.title: Germany funds 100 Humvee-sized heavy robots for Ukraine
articles.body:
- Ukraine's National Guard received the first 10 of 100 Protector heavy ground robots contracted with German government funding.
- The Humvee-sized vehicles are used for frontline logistics and casualty evacuation, with a payload capacity of 1,480 kilograms in this configuration.
Ukraine’s National Guard just started fielding a robot roughly the size of a Humvee, built to haul ammunition into combat zones so soldiers don’t have to.
Four units of Ukraine’s National Guard have received the first batch of Protector ground robotic complexes, part of a 100-unit contract funded by the German government, the National Guard said. Manufacturer Ukrainian Armor confirmed on X that the first 10 vehicles have already been produced and delivered.
This isn’t a small scout drone rolling on toy-sized wheels. The Protector is one of Ukraine’s largest unmanned ground vehicles, built on a diesel off-road chassis and weighing up to 4,000 kilograms (8,818 pounds), roughly in the weight class of a Humvee. It measures more than five meters (16.6 feet) long and stands nearly two meters (6.5 feet) wide, powered by a 190-horsepower engine.
Ukrainian Armor lists the payload capacity for the version supplied to the National Guard at 1,480 kilograms (3,263 pounds), one of the highest figures among current robotic logistics platforms, and higher than the 700-kilogram rating listed for earlier Protector configurations sold through Ukraine’s Brave1 Market platform, where the vehicle has been listed at $90,000. The National Guard version can also tow a trailer weighing up to 4 tonnes (4.4 tons), adding even more cargo capacity per trip. Soldiers from a separate Ukrainian brigade using the Protector have reported hauling nearly a metric ton of supplies in a single run, enough to resupply a frontline unit for roughly a week.
“Our logistics UGV has already proven itself well in military units subordinate to the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine,” said Vladyslav Belbas, general director of Ukrainian Armor. “Based on positive feedback from military personnel and understanding the need to protect people at the front, partners have contracted 100 of our complexes for the National Guard of Ukraine. Robotizing logistics allows important tasks to be carried out without unnecessary risk to personnel.”
The Protector’s core job is to keep soldiers away from the most dangerous stretch of road on the battlefield, the final approach into frontline positions. Beyond carrying ammunition, food, fuel and engineering supplies, the vehicle can evacuate wounded soldiers, removing them from combat zones without putting a driver at risk. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense codified the Protector in June 2025, and the vehicle entered serial production within two months. Depending on the configuration ordered, the platform can also carry electronic warfare equipment, a drone launch catapult, or remote weapon modules, including a version fitted with a 12.7mm Browning M2 machine gun known as the Tavria-12.7.
A Protector is already in frontline use with a separate National Guard artillery brigade and is set to be deployed to the Dobropillia sector, according to the National Guard.
“The complex has already proven itself well in our brigade,” said Sgt. Yevhen Kocherhin of that artillery brigade. “I especially want to note the sensitivity and smoothness of control in conditions far from ideal. The power, speed and payload capacity speak for themselves. For our artillery brigade, one of the key tasks is transporting heavy ammunition, and this is exactly where the Protector can significantly reduce risks to personnel.”
The vehicle’s size hasn’t made it invincible. Protector units operated by other Ukrainian formations, including the 429th Separate Unmanned Systems Brigade “Achilles,” have previously survived FPV drone strikes mid-mission and still completed their deliveries, though other units have been damaged beyond recovery by mines while returning from resupply runs.

articles.title: Sweden signs deal for four French FDI frigates
articles.body:
Sweden has signed a contract with France’s Naval Group for four FDI-based air defence frigates, completing a competition that also included British-Swedish and Spanish proposals, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The Swedish Defence Materiel Administration signed the procurement contract on 31 August during a visit to Stockholm by French President Emmanuel Macron, with the ships to enter Swedish service as the Luleå class.
The first frigate is planned for delivery in 2030, with the remaining three following successively. Sweden had selected Naval Group’s Frégate de Défense et d’Intervention design in May and subsequently entered negotiations with France over the purchase.
The Swedish Government said construction of the vessels and training of Swedish Armed Forces personnel can now begin following signature of the agreement.
Swedish Defence Minister Pål Jonson said: “This is a strategically important investment that strengthens Sweden’s defence capability and security in light of a deteriorated international situation. The four frigates will triple Sweden’s current air defence capability. This is essential to Sweden’s security and NATO’s capability.”
The Luleå-class vessels will be based on Naval Group’s FDI design but configured for Swedish requirements. The Swedish Government has previously confirmed that the ships will incorporate a number of domestically produced systems.
These are expected to include Saab’s RBS 15 anti-ship missile, lightweight torpedo, Giraffe 1X radar and Trackfire remote weapon station, together with 57mm and 40mm naval guns from BAE Systems Bofors.
The ships will also be equipped for area air defence. The Swedish Government said in May that advanced air defence was a central requirement for the programme and that the new frigates would contribute to NATO’s integrated air and missile defence capability.
Naval Group Chairman and Chief Executive Pierre Éric Pommellet said when the design was selected in May: “We are extremely honoured to have been selected by the Swedish Ministry of Defence. We are now eager to engage with the Swedish authorities and partners in the execution of this strategic project.”
He added: “The FDI will provide the Royal Swedish Navy with a latest-generation frigate and extended capabilities in all warfare domains with rapid delivery timeline, to meet the operational needs expressed by the Ministry of Defence.”
Naval Group faced two other proposals during the Swedish evaluation. Babcock, working with Swedish defence company Saab, offered the Arrowhead 120, a smaller derivative of the Arrowhead family that also includes the 140-metre design forming the basis of the Royal Navy’s Type 31 frigates.
The Arrowhead 120 proposed for Sweden is approximately 124 metres long and displaces around 4,650 tonnes. Babcock’s proposed configuration included the Saab 9LV combat management system, Sea Giraffe 4A fixed-face radar, Sea Giraffe 1X, RBS 15 anti-ship missiles, Saab lightweight torpedoes and Bofors guns.
Babcock and Saab had already been working on the Luleå programme before Sweden moved towards purchasing an existing foreign design. Saab had been contracted by the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration to undertake basic design work, with Babcock providing engineering support including structural design and auxiliary systems.
The third contender was Navantia’s ALFA 4000. The Spanish shipbuilder offered a 120-metre, approximately 4,300-tonne frigate and had proposed delivering the first two vessels in 2030 and the remaining pair in 2031.
Navantia’s proposed Swedish configuration also incorporated Swedish equipment, including the RBS 15, Bofors 57mm and 40mm guns and Saab Trackfire weapon stations. The company proposed air-defence, anti-submarine and surface-warfare capabilities alongside a hangar and flight deck suitable for helicopters.
Swedish officials said during the competition that the three proposals were assessed against time, capability and price. The government had also stipulated that the programme should concentrate on a mature vessel already in production in order to reduce delivery times.
The FDI is already in production for France and Greece. Naval Group pointed to the maturity of the production line and existing deliveries when making its Swedish proposal. The Swedish Government initially authorised negotiations with France in May for four ships expected to be delivered between 2030 and 2034. At the time, it said the procurement was the first stage of the process and that an order could be placed once negotiations were complete.
That process concluded with the contract signed on 31 August between the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration and Naval Group. Sweden and France also signed a separate framework agreement covering defence cooperation during Macron’s visit, including operational matters, defence equipment and industrial development.

articles.title: British warship makes first visit to Ream Naval Base
articles.body:
British patrol ship HMS Tamar has become the first Royal Navy warship to visit Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base, conducting joint training with Cambodian personnel during a week-long visit to the country.
The Royal Navy said the visit was HMS Tamar‘s first to Cambodia and the third call by a British warship to the country in three years, continuing engagement previously undertaken by sister ship HMS Spey.
Tamar spent the week in Sihanoukville, around 130 miles southwest of Phnom Penh, with activities including military training, meetings with Cambodian naval leaders and engagement with local organisations.
The ship was escorted into Ream Naval Base by two Cambodian patrol craft before being met by a guard of honour on the jetty. Commander Tom Lindsey, Commanding Officer of HMS Tamar, subsequently held discussions with Royal Cambodian Navy representatives covering current and potential future cooperation between the two services.
The visit follows a period of renewed Royal Navy engagement with Cambodia after an absence lasting more than six decades. Lindsey said in the Royal Navy release: “My ship’s company pulled out all the stops in welcoming key leaders from Cambodia’s Royal Navy, government officials, local school children and families.”
He added: “In doing so we showcased what Britain can offer and allowed us to message the importance of prosperity in this region to the UK’s own security and prosperity, enabled through maritime trade. Our respect for sovereignty and the rules-based system, which supports peaceful resolution through dialogue, is part of our national character and is a key part of our mission here in the Indo-Pacific.”
Cambodian sailors joined their British counterparts aboard Tamar for medical and damage-control training, including trauma care at sea and procedures for responding to flooding aboard a vessel.
The patrol ship also hosted a reception attended by government officials, military representatives, diplomats, business figures and regional leaders.
Lindsey said: “This visit was a great opportunity for my ship’s company to undertake defence engagement in a manner close to their hearts: through sports, including football and volleyball games alongside the Royal Cambodian Navy, with a celebratory barbecue afterwards, and through community outreach supporting a local children’s charity.”
He described the call at Ream as particularly notable for the ship, adding: “It has been a privilege to bring Tamar to Cambodia for the first time – and for it to be the Royal Navy’s first visit to Ream Naval Base makes it doubly special.”
The Royal Cambodian Navy operates a fleet of around 20 vessels, according to the Royal Navy, consisting mainly of patrol craft and landing vessels alongside the corvette Koh Kong Senchey.
Its roles include coastal security, counter-smuggling, counter-narcotics work, action against people trafficking and piracy, and search and rescue operations supporting fishermen. Members of Tamar‘s ship’s company also visited the M’lop Tapang organisation in Sihanoukville, which provides shelter and other support for children and young people. Sailors carried out maintenance and painting work at the organisation’s facilities.
Leading Medical Assistant Stanex said in the release: “A personal highlight for me was going to the children’s charity centre to paint the recreation area because we got to help those who had nothing and see the joy in the kids’ faces as we worked together to brighten up the area.”
HMS Tamar is one of the Royal Navy’s Batch 2 River-class offshore patrol vessels and has been deployed to the Indo-Pacific alongside HMS Spey on a long-term basis.
The two ships undertake maritime security cooperation, defence engagement, humanitarian assistance and disaster relief activity, and work intended to counter illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing across the region. The Cambodian visit concluded with further engagement between the two navies, including football and volleyball matches followed by a joint barbecue, before Tamar continued its wider Indo-Pacific deployment.

articles.title: Zelenskyy claims that Putin 'personally wants more war'
articles.body:
Kanyshai Butun
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed Monday that Russian President Vladimir Putin is “personally” interested in continuing the war between the two countries, a conflict now well into its fifth year.
In an evening address, Zelenskyy also said that an “absolute majority” of Putin’s “own society” would agree to stop the war along the line of contact.
“For now, unfortunately, all the intel – both ours and our partners’ – and all the signals from Russia indicate that the Russian leader personally wants more war,” he said.
Zelenskyy added that he had a phone call with US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner to discuss preparations for a meeting and further communication with the Russian side, as well as a potential visit by them to Ukraine.
“We discussed what could be done to encourage Russia to move toward ending the war,” he said. “The mood needs to be appropriate in Moscow, with Putin. A mood to end the war, not to wage it.”
“We will see what the representatives of the American president manage to achieve. September may change a lot,” he added.

articles.title: Iran warns any new US attack will trigger ‘much heavier’ response
articles.body:
Tarek Chouiref
01 September 2026•Update: 01 September 2026
Iran warned Monday that any site used to launch US attacks on its territory would be targeted, accusing Washington of continuing to use the territory, airspace, and facilities of regional countries to launch strikes on Iran.
Iran’s Armed Forces General Staff and the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters issued the warning in a joint statement, saying the US had continued such operations despite previous warnings and assurances from some countries in the region.
The two military bodies said Tehran respects the sovereignty of neighboring states but “will never tolerate aggression,” warning that any further attack would draw a “much heavier” response.
They pointed to attacks carried out overnight by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Iranian army as an example of that response.
“The US has no choice but to leave the region,” the statement said.
It also warned those facilitating US military action that the IRGC and Iranian army would jointly strike the source of any attack with “overwhelming force.”
“Do not test” the resolve of Iran’s armed forces again, the statement added.
On Sunday, US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island near the Strait of Hormuz, killing two people and injuring two others, according to Iranian media.
Iran subsequently announced retaliatory attacks against sites used by US forces in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates.

articles.title: Iran president meets PM Modi, seeks help to end war
articles.body:
File Photo: PM Modi holds a bilateral meeting with the President of Iran, Masoud Pezeshkian, on the sidelines of the SCO Summit, in Bishkek
In a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the margins of the SCO summit in Bishkek, PM Modi called for freedom of navigation and commerce while stressing that civilians and civilian infrastructure, including commercial shipping, and seafarers, must not be harmed under any circumstances. Despite the threat of US sanctions, both of them backed efforts to expand trade ties.The two discussed the West Asia situation, including the Strait of Hormuz and Chabahar port cooperation, in what was their first bilateral meeting in nearly two years. Pezeshkian urged Modi to use India's "extensive" contacts to wean away parties involved in the war.PM Modi expressed concern over escalation of tensions and reiterated the significance of resolving all issues through dialogue and diplomacy, while seeking lasting peace and stability in the region.Pezeshkian blamed the US for failing to fulfil its commitments and said continuation of the war was not in the interests of humanity.He urged Modi to use India’s “extensive” contacts to wean away the parties involved from the path of bloodshed and war. The President also called for expanding bilateral cooperation in political, economic, scientific, cultural and other areas of mutual interest, saying this would neutralise the impact of sanctions and further elevate the relationship.
Modi and Pezeshkian last had a bilateral meeting on the margins of the Brics summit in Kazan in 2024. The meeting gave both leaders an opportunity to reaffirm their commitment to expanding economic cooperation. Modi underlined India’s commitment to strengthening its long-standing “friendship” with Iran across diverse sectors. “We want to expand and diversify our trade basket in the times to come. We had a discussion on the prevailing situation in the region.
India will continue to support all efforts aimed at ensuring lasting peace,” said Modi in a post on X.According to an Iranian readout, Pezeshkian told Modi that despite efforts by the US and Israel to hamper Iran’s ties with other countries, Tehran was ready to expand cooperation with India across various fields.Modi also reiterated India’s readiness to cooperate closely with Iran in multilateral organisations, including Brics and SCO, and told Pezeshkian he was looking forward to welcoming him for the Brics Summit in India.“I am confident that your efforts will ultimately lead to positive results,” said PM Modi in the meeting, according to the Iranian readout.
