US steps up purchases of key Russian commodity – trade official
The US has stepped up purchases of Russian fertilizers despite broader Western restrictions on Moscow, with shipments rising by nearly a quarter in the first half of 2026, according to the Russia’s Export Center.
Veronika Nikishina, the center’s head, told RIA Novosti on Monday that the overall distribution of fertilizer exports had changed little since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. The US now ranks third among destinations for Russian supplies, she said, while Western Europe remains a larger market despite a decline in shipments this year.
Russia is the world’s largest exporter of fertilizers and one of the biggest producers, making its supplies difficult to replace on international markets. Fertilizer exports from the country were not directly targeted by Western sanctions, although broader restrictions on banking, shipping, and insurance have complicated trade. Moscow has meanwhile redirected a larger share of deliveries toward BRICS nations and the Global South.
“Sanctions against Russian fertilizers could have devastating consequences because of their importance to global food security. Even hardliners in unfriendly countries understand this,” Nikishina said.
US customs data cited by RIA in July showed that American fertilizer imports from Russia reached a record $1.04 billion between January and May, up 28% from a year earlier. Russia was the second-largest supplier to the US over that period after Canada, the figures showed.
In 2022, Washington authorized transactions involving Russian agricultural commodities including fertilizers to reduce the risk of shortages. The EU by contrast began imposing additional tariffs on some Russian nitrogen fertilizers in July 2025 as part of its drive to reduce reliance on Moscow, with the levies due to rise to €430 ($500) per ton by 2028.
The US-Israeli war on Iran and the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz have further exacerbated pressure on global fertilizer markets. The waterway handles an estimated third of the world’s fertilizer trade and a fifth of LNG shipments – a key input in the production of nitrate fertilizers. Experts, including Heartland Institute adviser Jeff Stier, have warned that any simultaneous disruption in the strait, the Black Sea, and to supplies from other major producers could trigger shortages of crop nutrients and a delayed food-price shock.

articles.title: how architecture has made space for animals across history
articles.body:
the nonhuman client was there before multispecies design
Long before architects began adding bird bricks, bee hotels and wildlife corridors to contemporary buildings, animals were already helping determine the shape of architecture. Across Europe, Asia and the Middle East, buildings were designed to accommodate pigeons, silkworms, horses, cattle and wild birds as part of systems that connected shelter, agriculture, religion, labor and power. The history of these structures suggests that the idea of multispecies architecture is a rediscovery of an older condition, as human buildings have always been influenced by nonhuman bodies.
A pigeon tower in Safavid Iran could turn the free movement of birds into agricultural fertilizer; a farmhouse in Edo-period Japan could use the heat generated by a household fire to sustain silkworm production; an Ottoman mosque might incorporate small sanctuaries for birds into its facade. Elsewhere, animal architecture expressed feudal privilege or increasingly industrial systems of extraction. Seen together, these buildings complicate the contemporary image of architecture as a purely human domain, asking, when architecture makes room for animals, who ultimately benefits from that space?
Mardavij Pigeon Tower walls | image by Գարվիք, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
pigeon towers turn animal behavior into infrastructure
Across the agricultural landscape around Isfahan, Safavid pigeon towers, or kabootar khaneh, housed large colonies of pigeons while serving a practical role in agriculture. The mudbrick structures provided protected nesting spaces, while the birds continued to fly out and forage across the surrounding landscape. Inside, rows of nesting niches filled the thick cylindrical walls. The towers protected the birds from predators and made it possible to collect their droppings, which were used as fertilizer and, in some cases, as a source of saltpeter.
The architecture was closely tied to the behavior of the pigeons. The size and arrangement of the nesting spaces, along with openings for birds to enter and ventilation through the tower, were all part of keeping the colonies healthy and productive. At the same time, the birds connected the building to the surrounding farmland, where they fed before returning to roost. The pigeons were given a protected place to nest because their presence produced something useful: fertilizer and other agricultural resources.
Shirakawa-go | image by lumoplank, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
in japan, the farmhouse becomes a thermal system for silkworms
The gasshō-zukuri farmhouses of Shirakawa-gō and Gokayama are large timber houses built in the snowy mountains of central Japan, where domestic life and silkworm farming took place under the same roof. Their steep thatched roofs are perhaps their most recognizable feature, but the upper floors were also important for sericulture. Silkworms were raised in the attic spaces, while the hearth on the floor below provided heat that rose through the house.
Cooking, heating and silk production were therefore closely connected. The arrangement made the farmhouse a home and a place of production. The household relied on sericulture for income, while the layout of the building helped create the conditions needed to raise the silkworms.
Shirakawa-go | image by lumoplank, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons
birdhouses turn the facade into shared urban space
The Ottoman kuş evleri, or birdhouses, offer a different approach to accommodating animals in the city. Built into the walls of mosques, fountains, libraries and other public buildings across Istanbul and other Ottoman cities, these small structures provided nesting spaces for birds. Some were designed as miniature versions of the buildings they were attached to, with tiny arches, roofs, ledges and other architectural details.
Builders deliberately incorporated nesting spaces into the architecture. Unlike dovecotes built for agriculture, these birdhouses were not primarily intended to produce meat or collect manure. Their presence was connected instead to religious and charitable traditions that encouraged care for animals. The small structures brought animal life into prominent public spaces, making birds a visible part of the city.
In Ahmedabad and elsewhere in Gujarat, the chabutro offers a different way of making space for animals in the city. These elevated bird-feeding structures are found within residential neighborhoods, providing food, water and shelter for wild birds. Their raised platforms help protect the birds from predators while keeping them close to the center of daily urban life.
Carved timber and stone, shaded platforms and projecting roofs give the structures a distinct presence within the neighborhood. The chabutro is notable for placing space for birds directly within the city, making feeding and caring for birds part of the shared public environment, a tradition also connected to Jain ideas of ahiṃsā, or non-violence, and compassion toward living beings.
Ayazma Mosque birdhouse | image by R Prazeres, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
ANIMAL ARCHITECTURE AND ARISTOCRATIC POWER
The French colombier and the Grandes Écuries at the Château de Chantilly show how animal buildings could also express wealth and social status. In early modern France, dovecotes were closely tied to seigneurial power and the droit de colombier, which gave certain landowners the right to keep pigeons. Their circular walls contained rows of nesting niches, while rotating ladders allowed keepers to reach the birds. Openings connected the pigeons to the surrounding fields, where they could forage before returning to the estate. Their meat and droppings then became part of the landowner’s economy.
The colombier at the Manoir d’Ango in Normandy makes this relationship particularly visible. Its elaborate construction served the practical needs of pigeon keeping, but its scale and ornament also reflected the status of its owner. The building was part of the estate’s architecture and its system of land ownership.
At Chantilly, this relationship takes on a much larger scale. Designed by Jean Aubert between 1719 and 1735 for Louis-Henri de Bourbon, Prince of Condé, the Grandes Écuries gave horses an architectural setting more commonly associated with palaces and monumental buildings than agricultural structures. Its vaulted interiors and extensive stone construction reflected the importance of horses to aristocratic life.
Colombier du manoir d’Ango | image by Louistisserand, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
the model farm turns animals into measurable units
By the nineteenth century, animal housing was becoming more standardized. The British Model Farm movement focused on ventilation, sanitation and making farm work more efficient. John Claudius Loudon’s writings helped establish a more systematic approach to farm buildings, with cattle, pigs and other livestock housed in spaces designed around feeding, waste removal, ventilation and productivity. This was a shift from the more integrated arrangement of earlier buildings. In the gasshō-zukuri farmhouse, domestic life and silkworm production were closely connected. Model Farms instead treated animals as things that could be measured and managed. The buildings were designed to control the conditions around the animals. Ventilation regulated the air, drainage removed waste, and feeding systems reduced the amount of labor needed to care for livestock. Materials and construction methods could also be used to control temperature. The animal was increasingly treated as part of a system of inputs and outputs: feed, heat, space and labor were calculated against the amount of meat, milk or other products produced. This approach helped establish the spatial logic of modern industrial agriculture, in which animal production became increasingly separated from everyday urban life.
Grandes Écuries, Château de Chantilly, France | P.poschadel, CC BY-SA 2.0 FR, via Wikimedia Commons
MULTISPECIES ARCHITECTURE AS A RETURN TO AN OLDER IDEA
Seen against this history, today’s interest in multispecies architecture begins to look less like a new idea and more like a return to a relationship that modern architecture has largely left behind. For centuries, animals were part of the spaces people lived and worked in, whether they were producing food and materials, contributing to household economies, protected for religious reasons, or serving as markers of wealth and status. Industrialization changed that relationship, moving animal production into increasingly controlled spaces and separating it from everyday urban life.
Looking at these buildings as animal habitats complicates the idea that multispecies architecture begins with contemporary ecological design. Some shelter birds without extracting anything from them, others depend on animals for food or agricultural production, while others turn animal housing into an expression of wealth and power. What they share is a recognition that architecture can create conditions for another species to live. The question contemporary architecture inherits is what those habitats are designed to do and what kind of relationship they establish with the animals that occupy them.
Chabutra in Ahmedabad | image by Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
This article is part of designboom’s MODES OF HABITATION chapter, exploring how the spaces we inhabit can reshape the ways we live together. Discover more stories rethinking domesticity, shared living, and the many forms a home can take here.

articles.title: Rolls-Royce completes $1bn US defence investment
articles.body:
Rolls-Royce has completed a decade-long $1 billion investment programme in Indiana, expanding manufacturing, assembly and engine-test facilities supporting US military aircraft including the B-52, C-130J, V-22 and MQ-25A, according to the company.
Rolls-Royce announced completion of the programme on 27 August, describing it as the largest investment the company has made in the United States.
The work has modernised manufacturing facilities across the company’s Indianapolis campus and added full engine-test capability. It also includes new ground-test facilities and an altitude-test facility at West Lafayette. Rolls-Royce said more of its defence products are now built in Indianapolis than at any other company site worldwide.
Adam Riddle, President of Defence and Chief Executive Officer of Rolls-Royce North America, said in the company release: “This billion-dollar investment is about more than buildings and test cells — it is about delivering for the American warfighter, on time and at the standard our customers expect. We made this investment because it was the right thing to do for U.S. national security and for the future of Rolls-Royce.”
The Indianapolis site builds and tests engines for a range of current and future US military aircraft. Rolls-Royce identified future propulsion work for the US Air Force’s B-52 strategic bomber and the US Army’s MV-75 Cheyenne among the programmes supported by the campus.
Current production also supports the V-22 Osprey, Lockheed Martin C-130J and the US Navy’s MQ-25A Stingray uncrewed carrier-based tanker. The investment therefore spans both established fleets and aircraft currently entering or preparing for future service, with the Indiana facilities covering manufacturing as well as assembly and testing.
Rolls-Royce employs approximately 3,500 people in Indianapolis, including a unionised manufacturing workforce, and says its operations support additional employment through suppliers elsewhere in Indiana. Indiana Governor Mike Braun said in the release: “Rolls-Royce has called Indiana home for three decades, and this billion-dollar investment is a vote of confidence in Hoosier workers and our state.”
He added: “Advanced manufacturing like this is exactly what keeps Indiana’s economy strong and growing. We are proud that Indiana is home to Rolls-Royce in the U.S., and we look forward to their continued success for generations to come.”
The company has also invested elsewhere in its American industrial base. According to Rolls-Royce, expenditure over the past decade amounts to more than $1.5 billion across US facilities and almost $2.5 billion in research and development.
The Indianapolis campus is also home to LibertyWorks, Rolls-Royce’s advanced research organisation. Its work includes propulsion technologies and high-temperature materials, supported in part through a $75 million, ten-year research alliance with Purdue University.
US Senator Todd Young said: “This investment is a testament to the hard-working Hoosiers who power this facility. Rolls-Royce understands the importance of producing advanced military technologies here in the United States, and this billion-dollar investment shows that Indiana is leading the way in meeting the needs of our defense industrial base.”

articles.title: US uses fewer weapons against Iran than provided to Ukraine under Biden — Trump
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, September 1. /TASS/. Washington has used fewer weapons in its conflict with Iran than the amount provided to Ukraine under former US President Joe Biden, current US leader Donald Trump told reporters.
"This is a relatively little war for us. This is not a big war," he said, referring to the Iran operation. "You know where the money went was Ukraine," Trump stressed.
"They say we used it [ammunition] in Iran. We used very little in Iran by comparison. Joe Biden gave Ukraine over $300 billion worth of stuff free. Now, I also help Ukraine, but they have to pay for it. So Europe is paying for it. It goes to the European nations. It goes to NATO. They pay us for it, and we help them out. But he gave away 300 billion dollars worth of ammunition. That’s… Can’t do that," Trump noted.

articles.title: Cultural association brings Taiwan to Poland
articles.body:
The National Cultural Association of Taiwan (NCAT) is planning a two-day “Taiwan Day” cultural event in Poland on Sept. 11 and 12, featuring Taiwanese contemporary dance and folk arts, as well as a bazaar showcasing Taiwanese food and culture.
Events on the first day are being held in Lodz in central Poland, with performances by the Lei Sheng Art Group, a Taiwanese folk arts group, and Taipei Gong Le Xuan, a Taiwanese beiguan music ensemble.
The performances would “transform the Polish streets into a Taiwan temple front,” according to a social media post by the association yesterday.
Photo : CNA
There would be a bazaar with more than 10 vendors showcasing Taiwanese foods and goods, including dumplings, sometimes called a Taiwanese analogue to Polish pierogi. There would also be offerings of bubble tea and Taiwanese tea, the post said.
On Sept. 12, the two groups would be joined by the MeimageDance Troupe, founded by choreographer and National Award for Arts winner Ho Hsiao-mei (何曉玫), for performances in Opole in southwestern Poland, according to the post.
MeimageDance is also to perform in Austria on Sept. 5 and in Hungary on Sept. 18 and 19, the post said.
At a promotional event in Taipei Monday, Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴), who serves as NCAT vice president, said the cultural tour is aimed at inspiring Europeans to visit Taiwan and experience the country in person.
Taiwan is a resilient and diverse society with a wide range of folk beliefs, contemporary arts and distinctive foods such as bubble tea and xiaolongbao, all of which are part of the everyday experiences and shared memories of the people of Taiwan, Hsiao said.
While Taiwan faces difficulties in its diplomatic relations, its goodwill toward the world has never wavered, Hsiao said, adding that she hoped cultural diplomacy could help deepen the international community’s understanding of Taiwan.

articles.title: IISc sets up quantum computing hub under National Quantum Mission
articles.body:
The new Section 8 company will serve as the Quantum Computing Thematic Hub at IISc under the Union Govt’s National Quantum Mission
BENGALURU: IISc has set up a not-for-profit company to help build India’s capabilities in quantum computing, a technology expected to play a role in areas ranging from scientific research and industry to computing and communications in the coming years.Called the Foundation for QC Innovation (FQCI), the new Section 8 company will serve as the Quantum Computing Thematic Hub at IISc under the Union Govt’s National Quantum Mission.It’s one of four thematic hubs set up under the mission and will bring together researchers, academic institutions, industry and startups to develop quantum computing technologies in India.Quantum computers use the principles of quantum physics to process certain kinds of information differently from conventional computers. While the technology is still at an early stage, countries and companies around the world are investing heavily in it because of its potential to solve some problems that are difficult for existing computers.At IISc, the new hub will work across several approaches to building quantum computers, including systems based on light particles, superconducting circuits, semiconductor devices, neutral atoms and trapped ions.
It will also work on quantum algorithms.“The National Quantum Mission provides a unique opportunity to build a strong and globally competitive quantum computing ecosystem in India. Our focus is on bringing together India’s research capabilities, advanced infrastructure, industry and entrepreneurial talent to translate cutting-edge research into indigenous quantum computing technologies and applications,” Shankar Kumar Selvaraja, project director, FQCI and professor, Centre for Nano Science and Engineering at IISc, said.
A major part of the initiative will be the creation of shared facilities for making, testing and characterising quantum devices. The aim is to give researchers and companies access to infrastructure that can help move laboratory research towards working technologies.“FQCI will also focus on building the workforce and startup ecosystem required for the sector. Its programmes will support student research and internships, industry-academia collaboration, startup development and knowledge-sharing. The initiative has launched programmes called QC Rise, QC Bridge, QC Leap, QC Accel and QC Quest as part of these efforts,” IISc said.The larger goal, it added, was to reduce dependence on overseas technology by developing quantum computing capabilities within the country.

articles.title: Unwave Gives Mesh-Network Anti-Drone EW Systems to Ukrainian Railways
articles.body:
Ukrainian Railways received SHATRO COUNTER-MESH electronic warfare systems free of charge.
The systems are designed to protect rolling stock and critical infrastructure facilities from UAVs using mesh networks, Ukrainian company Unwave told Militarnyi.
Ukrainian Railways officially confirmed the system’s high effectiveness in real-world operating conditions.
The first systems were handed over to railway workers for trial operation at the end of June. Enemy UAVs equipped with mesh modems were detected within the systems’ coverage area at distances of 500 to 1,500 meters.
As they entered the system’s operating area, Russian drones changed their flight paths.
The SHATRO COUNTER-MESH suppresses communication links between a UAV’s mesh modem and other network nodes at a range of up to 1,000 meters. This prevents command transmission and disrupts drone coordination.
The Ukrainian electronic warfare system developed by Unwave was the only system capable of jamming a UAV during the NATO Baltic Trust 26 exercise in Latvia.

articles.title: Philosopher’s Annual for 2025
articles.body:
Philosopher’s Annual for 2025
The articles that made it into the latest edition of Philosophers Annual have been announced.
The list aims to “select the ten best articles published in philosophy each year—an attempt as simple to state as it is admittedly impossible to fulfill.”
This volume—the 45th—covers the literature from 2025.
The selections are:
Evan Behrle (Harvard), “Desert and Economic Interdependence” from the Journal of Philosophy.
Outside of philosophy, the idea that workers deserve to be paid according to their productive contributions is very popular. But political philosophers have given it relatively little attention. In this paper, I argue against the attempt to use this idea about desert and contribution to vindicate significant income inequality. I claim that reward according to contribution fails on its own terms when the following condition holds: the size of each worker’s contribution depends on what other workers only together do. When workers only together make another more productive, that is not reflected in the sum of their own contributions. Thus reward according to contribution recognizes individual accomplishments without recognizing their dependence on collectives, dependence that is, in complex economies, ubiquitous.
Sam Berstler (MIT), “The Structure of Open Secrets” from the Philosophical Review.
In conversation, we often do not acknowledge what we jointly know to be true. This article identifies a distinctive kind of non-acknowledgment norm, open secrecy norms, and analyzes how such norms constrain our speech. First, the author argues that open secrecy norms are structurally different from other everyday non-acknowledgment norms. Open secrecy norms iterate: when is an open secret, then there’s a norm not to acknowledge that , and this norm is itself an open secret. Then, the author argues that the non-acknowledgment at issue in open secrecy norms motivates a more complex understanding of discourse structure. When interlocutors are conforming to open secrecy norms, they rely on at least two disjoint common grounds, one of which has a privileged status. To understand why and how it is privileged, the author develops Erving Goffman’s notion of defining a social interaction. Finally, the author shows how strategic speakers can exploit the structure of open secrecy norms in order to both communicate about the open secret and shield themselves from retaliation for what they communicate.
Kyle Blumberg (Melbourne) and Ben Holguín (Johns Hopkins), “Fictional Reality” from the Philosophical Review.
This article defends a theory of fictional truth. According to this theory, there is a fact of the matter concerning the number of hairs on Sherlock Holmes’s head, and likewise for any other meaningful question one could ask about what’s true in a work of fiction. This article argues that a theory of this form is needed to account for the patterns in our judgments about attitude reports that embed fictional claims. It contrasts this view with one of the dominant approaches to fictional truth, which originates with David Lewis. Along the way it explores the relationship between fiction, counterfactuals, and vagueness.
Liam Kofi Bright (LSE), Nathan Gabriel (UC Merced), Cailin O’Connor (UC Irvine), and Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò (Georgetown), “On the Stability of Racial Capitalism” from Ergo.
What is the connection between capitalism and racial hierarchy? In line with the tradition known as ‘the theory of racial capitalism’ we show that the latter can functionally support the former. As a social construction, race has just those features which allow it to facilitate the sort of stable, inequitable distributions of resources that tend to emerge in capitalist systems. We support this claim using techniques from evolutionary game theory and cultural evolutionary theory, and end by discussing the normative political consequences of this relationship.
Colin Chamberlain (UCL), “How To Eat a Peach: Malebranche on the Function of the Passions” from Mind.
Nicolas Malebranche (1638-1715) holds that the senses, imagination, and passions serve the body’s needs. In this paper, I explain how the passions keep us alive by situating them in Malebranche’s account of ordinary bodily action. Malebranche holds a consent-based view of action. An agent translates her inclinations or motives into action only when she consents to them. The passions contribute to the preservation of life by helping the agent close the gap between inclination and action. The passions, according to Malebranche, are complex psychophysiological phenomena whose various elements—perceptions, shifts of attention, evaluations, bodily preparation, feelings, and so on—work together to elicit the agent’s consent.
Dai Heide (Simon Fraser), “The Transcendental Aesthetic and the Leibnizian Theory of Space” from the Journal of the History of Philosophy.
In considering Kant’s response to the Leibnizian theory of space in the Transcendental Aesthetic, scholars have overwhelmingly emphasized Kant’s response to Leibniz’s relationalism. They have largely missed the metaphysically realistic aspects of Leibniz’s theory with which Kant is primarily concerned. As such, scholars have failed to appreciate the threat Leibniz’s theory poses to Kant’s idealism, a point made publicly as early as 1786 by H. A. Pistorius. I argue that the Aesthetic does indeed contain a compelling argument against the Leibnizian theory of space. This argument crucially depends upon Kant’s claim that space is monistic: that the whole of space is prior to the parts of space and, as such, spatial representations are not decomposable.
Elselijn Kingma (KCL) and Fiona Woollard (Southampton), “Can You Do Harm to Your Fetus? Pregnancy, Barriers, and the Doing/Allowing Distinction” from Ethics.
When pregnant persons do not behave in the way deemed optimal for their fetus, they are often framed as doing harm. This framing acts as a justificatory bypass for defenses of widespread expectations of pregnant persons, allowing such defenses to avoid substantial questions about special obligations in pregnancy. Our main claim is that this justificatory bypass is unwarranted: in many cases either the pregnant person does not count as doing harm or substantive questions about special obligations cannot be avoided. Our secondary claim is that direct engagement with these substantive questions is unlikely to justify widespread expectations on pregnant people.
Alexander Meehan (Wisconsin) and Snow Zhang (UC Berkeley), “Bayes Is Back” from the Philosophical Review.
A core tenet of Bayesian epistemology is that Bayesian conditionalization is the rule of rational credal revision. But it has been pointed out in the recent literature that if learning can be nontransparent, then Bayesian conditionalization does not universally maximize expected accuracy. This result raises an explanatory challenge for any externalist Bayesian who does not want to give up on a connection between accuracy and epistemic rationality: Why is Bayesian conditionalization the rule of rational credal revision, despite the fact that it does not universally maximize expected accuracy? This article proposes an answer to this challenge. The article argues that an updating rule can be evaluated, not only on the basis of its expected accuracy in particular learning situations, but also on the basis of its total expected accuracy across different learning situations. The article proposes a notion of global evidential constancy, and shows that, out of all globally evidentially constant rules, Bayesian conditionalization has the highest total expected accuracy across all learning situations, including nontransparent ones. Bayes is back!
Paulina Sliwa (Vienna), “Changing Minds and Hearts” from Russ Shafer-Landau, ed., Oxford Studies in Metaethics, vol. 20.
Suppose you are uncertain about some moral question. Are you falling morally short, if you rely on moral advice? A popular line of thought is that the problem with relying on moral testimony is that it can change beliefs but not feelings. An agent who forms a moral judgment based on testimony will be emotionally alienated from the moral judgment they accept. They may come to believe—even know—that a given course of action is right or wrong. But they won’t feel it. The aim of this chapter is to challenge this diagnosis: that moral deference will leave the agent emotionally disconnected from the features that matter. It does so by examining the phenomenon of hermeneutical advice: this is moral testimony that aims at helping an agent to make sense of her moral situation. Hermeneutical advice, it is argued, has the power to change minds and hearts.
Quinn White (Harvard), “Love First” from Philosophy and Phenomenological Research.
How should we respond to the humanity of others? Should we care for others’ well-being? Respect them as autonomous agents? Largely neglected is an answer we can find in the religious traditions of Judaism, Christianity and Buddhism: we should love all. This paper argues that an ideal of love for all can be understood apart from its more typical religious contexts and moreover provides a unified and illuminating account of the the nature and grounds of morality. I defend a novel account of love for all that avoids serious worries about the incoherence or impossibility of loving everyone. Doing so requires countenancing a neglected form of love. Love admits as its object not just individual entities like people and groups; we can also bear a love for the Fs in general—for all the Joneses, all the philosophers, or even all the human beings. I go on to argue that while it is possible for ordinary agents like us to love all, we shouldn’t. Instead, we should approximate love for all. The minimal approximation of love for all is, surprisingly, respect; I derive the basic, structural features of deontological ethics (including anti-paternalism and anti-aggregation) from the ideal of loving all.

articles.title: India to get Javelin missile assembly facility
articles.body:
- Tata Advanced Systems and the Javelin Joint Venture signed an MOU to co-produce Javelin missiles in India.
- Sub-assembly kits and guidance electronics will continue to be built in Alabama and Arizona before final assembly in India.
Tata Advanced Systems Limited and the Javelin Joint Venture, a partnership between Raytheon and Lockheed Martin, signed a memorandum of understanding to co-produce the Javelin All Up Round missile in India, the companies announced Sunday.
Under the agreement, Tata Advanced Systems and the joint venture, known as JJV, will explore setting up a final assembly and integration facility in India for the Javelin round, along with local component production capabilities. Tata was selected as the prime partner for the effort after JJV evaluated multiple Indian companies based on capability and expertise.
The arrangement calls for Lockheed Martin’s facility in Troy, Alabama, to continue producing sub-assembly kits, while Raytheon’s facility in Tucson, Arizona, would continue building guidance electronics units. Those components would then be shipped to India for final assembly and integration, keeping the initial manufacturing work inside the existing U.S. supply chain while adding a final production step in India.
“Partnering with Tata Advanced Systems Limited to establish a dedicated Javelin final assembly and integration facility in India is a pivotal step in ensuring a resilient, supply chain for this critical anti-tank weapon system,” said Rich Liccion, vice president of JJV and program director for Lockheed Martin Javelin.
“This agreement with Tata Advanced Systems Limited establishes a foundation to strengthen the global supply chain for Javelin,” said Jenna Hunt Frazier, JJV president and Javelin program director at Raytheon. “It supports faster fielding of the proven Javelin weapon system and sustained readiness for partner nations.”
“We are pleased to partner with the Javelin Joint Venture on this important next step in our long-standing relationship with Lockheed Martin and Raytheon,” said Sukaran Singh, chief executive officer and managing director of Tata Advanced Systems Limited. “This initiative brings critical assembly expertise and knowledge transfer into India’s defence industrial ecosystem, while strengthening self-reliance. Local assembly of the Javelin All Up Round will enhance operational readiness and ensure timely access to proven, combat-ready capability for the Indian Armed Forces.”
The Javelin is a shoulder-fired, fire-and-forget anti-tank missile system. The JJV, split between Raytheon’s Tucson facility and Lockheed Martin’s plant in Orlando, Florida, has produced more than 55,000 Javelin missiles and more than 12,000 reusable Command Launch Units to date.
India’s military already operates the Javelin. The country signed a $125 million foreign military sale agreement with the U.S. in April 2025 to acquire Javelin missiles and launchers, following earlier trials the Indian Army conducted with the system.

The U.S. Department of Defense has concluded 7-year framework agreements with General Dynamics and Lockheed Martin to sharply increase the production of components for PAC-3 MSE and THAAD interceptor missiles. This was reported by the U.S. Department of Defense, according to UNN.

The new agreements provide for tripling production capacity for PAC-3 MSE interceptors, which are used in Patriot surface-to-air missile systems. At the same time, capacity for producing interceptors for the THAAD missile defense system is planned to increase fourfold.
In addition, the United States will increase production of key missile components, including motor casings, seeker-head elements, and fairing deployment systems.
The Pentagon wants to accelerate missile deliveries
We are cutting bureaucracy, shortening timelines, and rapidly scaling up our domestic production capacity to provide advanced air and missile defense capabilities
The Department of Defense explained that the long-term agreements would guarantee minimum annual procurement volumes. This should enable manufacturers to expand their workforce, purchase the necessary materials in advance, and modernize their production facilities.
Contract funding will depend on annual budget appropriations. The Pentagon expects the new procurement model to simultaneously increase production volumes and shorten delivery timelines for critical air and missile defense systems.

articles.title: Reuters: Ukrainian attacks are pushing Russian grain out of the Black Sea and into the Baltic
articles.body:
Reuters: Ukrainian attacks are pushing Russian grain out of the Black Sea and into the Baltic
Russian grain exporters have begun rerouting shipments from the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov to the Baltic Sea amid Ukrainian attacks on vessels and port infrastructure, according to Reuters.
In the last export season, from July 2025 to June 2026, Russia shipped 46.3 million tons of grain through its Black Sea and Azov ports — 90% of its seaborne exports. Its Baltic ports handled about 1 million tons.
But by August 18, rail booking requests for grain shipments to Russian Baltic ports this season had already reached 5 million tons, an industry source told Reuters, against 6 million tons for the Black Sea ports of Novorossiysk and Tuapse.
Russian exporters are increasingly looking to ports in the Baltic states, mainly Latvia. Russia’s Grain Union estimates exports through those ports could hit 5–6 million tons this season, or 10 million if Estonia opens up.
Strikes by the Ukrainian military have knocked out more than 80% of Russia’s grain export capacity. In August, wheat exports came to just 1.9 million tons, according to expert estimates — the lowest level in 16 years.

articles.title: Glacial flood death toll surpasses 900 in Nepal and Tibet
articles.body:
Glacial flood death toll surpasses 900 in Nepal and Tibet
Rescuers battled mud and debris Monday as the death toll from devastating glacial floods along the China-Nepal border topped 900, with nearly 4,500 people still missing. Rescue teams continued a desperate search for survivors as entire communities were swept away.

One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Rescuers struggled on Monday through mud and debris for a sixth day, as the number of missing people soared to nearly 4,500 since tsunami-like glacial floods roared down from the China-Nepal border, creating an "unimaginable" disaster.
The latest confirmed death toll surged above 900, with unidentified bodies buried in mass graves after DNA sampling.
The huge wave of freezing water, rocks and debris that smashed into villages and towns on Wednesday killed at least 939 people in Nepal and in Tibet, in China, with at least 17 bodies also pulled from rivers downstream in India.
Shibu Giri, a hydropower worker in Rasuwa, counts himself lucky to be alive.
A helicopter crew "tried to rescue me three times, but my body was stuck in the mud, up to my waist", the 44-year-old Nepali told AFP.
"I asked them to throw water and food," said Giri, who was eventually rescued and taken to hospital.
Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah on Sunday called the disaster "unimaginable and heartbreaking".
In Chitwan district, army personnel climbed out of rubber dinghies and carried dead victims in blue body bags up a river bank, placing them in a row along a dirt road.
Rescue teams are in a race against time in treacherous conditions to free around 100 hydropower workers believed trapped in multiple tunnels -- digging, drilling and blasting through debris.
So far, three bodies have been pulled from two tunnels, and the teams have found routes blocked with mud.
An Indian army officer deployed as part of a specialised tunnel rescue team said rescuers were digging through "sludge". He told AFP he was "still hopeful" there were survivors inside.
Nepal's Home Affairs Ministry says 20,600 personnel have been mobilised, and that more than 3,100 people have been rescued from the disaster zone.
Army personnel were seen unloading bodies of victims from helicopters in Nepal's Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts on Monday.
Amid the horror, there has been some hope; a six-year-old pulled out of the mud Friday was reunited with her parents after police found her crying for her mother.
"Her body was trapped in mud, but her head was outside," Nepali Armed Police spokesman Netra Bahadur Karki told AFP.
"She is out of danger and recovering at a hospital."
Read moreNepal grapples with destruction and loss in wake of deadly floods
'Changing climate'
The disaster was sparked by a glacial collapse, the US Geological Survey said.
Climate change is causing glaciers to melt worldwide, raising the risk of such disasters.
"The people of Nepal are one of the major victims of the changing climate and its impact," Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal said.
Scientists say the Himalayas, the world's highest mountain range, are melting faster as global temperatures rise.
Aid needs are enormous after entire communities were swept away.
"This is an unfolding disaster," UN children's fund official Abiodun Banire told AFP, saying the needs of the tens of thousands impacted were vast.
Roads have been wiped out, power plants destroyed and dozens of bridges smashed.
"There are too many challenges," said police officer E. Hawadi in badly affected Nuwakot district.
Overflowing mortuaries
With mortuaries overflowing, Nepal has begun burying some of the hundreds of bodies recovered -- after taking DNA samples so families can later retrieve them.
In Chitwan district, mourning relatives cremated some of the dead, while in riverside villages like Devighat, survivors were struggling to salvage any remaining belongings from their devastated homes.
Kathmandu has appealed for international support, saying Nepal needed "more than a thousand" freezer units to store bodies.
Distraught families watch images of bodies on screens at community centres in a bid to identify their loved ones.
Shobha Adhikary, in the southern Nepali city of Bharatpur, told a local coordinator she believed one image showed her childhood best friend.
"It looks like him, for sure," she said, showing a photograph of a smiling, middle-aged man.
Among Nepal's list of the missing are 592 foreigners, including tourists who had come for mountain trekking, as well as Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet's sacred Mount Kailash.
In China, Tibet is largely inaccessible to foreign journalists, and Chinese authorities are the only source of information.
Read moreNepal races to find its missing as flood area remains largely inaccessible
More than 2,000 personnel are part of rescue operations there, but they have faced intense challenges, and are slowly advancing towards the disaster's epicentre.
China has said 16 people died in Tibet, with 546 missing.
Tibetan advocacy groups in exile have questioned China's account of the disaster.
Tencho Gyatso, president of the International Campaign for Tibet, called for China to disclose "complete and verifiable information about the damage and casualties".
Beijing's foreign ministry said Monday that the "release of information has been open, transparent and timely", and rejected international reports it is underreporting deaths.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: US Army Secretary Driscoll submits resignation — newspaper

NEW YORK, September 1. /TASS/. US Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll has submitted his resignation to President Donald Trump following months of tension with Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, The Wall Street Journal reported.
Driscoll is expected to leave the Pentagon in the coming days, according to the newspaper.
"Secretary Driscoll has been highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda <...> by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine," the paper quoted White House Spokeswoman Anna Kelly as saying. "The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War," she added.
Last November, Trump included Driscoll in the US delegation involved in efforts to resolve the conflict in Ukraine. In February 2026, he took part in US-Russia-Ukraine talks in Geneva.

articles.title: Iran Foreign Ministry issues statement after US aggression

Iran's Foreign Ministry said Monday that U.S. forces attacked Larak island, martyring and wounding several Iranian military forces and civilians, and that Iran struck U.S. military bases in Jordan in response.
In a statement issued Monday morning, the ministry said the U.S. military struck parts of Larak island on Sunday evening, violating Iran's national sovereignty and territorial integrity. The attack left several "courageous defenders of the homeland and dear compatriots" martyred and wounded, and caused damage to public and private property, it said.
The ministry said Iranian armed forces, acting in accordance with the inherent right of self-defence, delivered "defensive and crushing blows" to U.S. military bases in Jordan, which it said was the origin and support of the U.S. military aggression against Iran.
The ministry strongly condemned the U.S. military attack on Larak as a clear violation of Article 2(4) of the UN Charter, and reminded the UN Security Council and the Secretary-General of their responsibility to uphold international peace and security and hold the aggressor accountable.
It told the UN Secretary-General, the Security Council president, and all governments that had expressed concern about insecurity in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz that the sole cause of the region's unsafe shipping routes had been "the illegal and aggressive actions of the United States and the Zionist regime," starting with the attack on Iran on February 28 and continuing for six months through the naval blockade and other provocative and interventionist measures.
The ministry stressed that Iran's armed forces "will not hesitate to exercise the inherent right of self-defence" and will respond decisively and appropriately to any enemy military aggression.
It said full responsibility for the consequences of new U.S. aggressive actions, the continued naval blockade and economic war against Iran rests with the "American regime" and all parties that participate in preparing and carrying out America's illegal actions.

articles.title: Reigning In Big Tech: How California lawmakers plan to regulate AI and social media
articles.body:
Reigning In Big Tech: How California lawmakers plan to regulate AI and social media
-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SACRAMENTO — Long the epicenter of the global tech industry, California is taking more action to shield its children, communities and workers from the threats posed by the very industry that’s become central to the state’s identity and enviable economy.
State lawmakers on Monday passed new safeguards around social media and artificial intelligence — and are poised to approve restrictions on data centers — at a time when technology has become intertwined with people’s daily lives.
Efforts to rein in the power of Big Tech extend beyond concerns that TikTok, Instagram and other social media platforms are harming young children.
Unions and workers worry that AI will take their jobs, and lawmakers are trying to tackle privacy and safety issues as AI features get added into smart glasses and toys. Californians are concerned that the proliferation of data centers will increase their electricity bills and strain water supplies.
“There’s a heightened level of tech anxiety right now, and that manifests itself from social media to data centers to AI taking jobs,” said Assemblyman Josh Lowenthal (D-Long Beach). “People are coalescing and they’re demanding that policymakers make change.”
California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who has previously vetoed some bills aimed at adding restrictions on Silicon Valley businesses, will still have to weigh in on whether to sign the pieces of legislation into law.
The Democratic governor has acknowledged the challenge of adopting regulations that protect the public without going too far and potentially stifling the technology industry’s growth, which brings critical revenue to the state budget.
“I think that’s the constant tension,” Newsom said in an interview earlier this summer. “We’re constantly sort of fighting that balance.”
The governor, who has close relationships in the technology industry from his time in San Francisco, said only a couple other states have attempted to regulate artificial intelligence like California. The state, he said, leads on regulation of social media.
“We’re not rolling over, certainly,” Newsom said. “We’re leaning forward, and we’re iterating. We will push the boundaries and litigate.”
The looming restrictions on social media follow a landmark Meta Platforms legal settlement aimed at making social media safer for young people. Parents, politicians and child advocacy groups are worried that social media is contributing to depression, anxiety, eating disorders and other issues.
The actions being pushed in the California Legislature are more sweeping than that settlement, however. One of the bills passed by lawmakers on Monday, Assembly Bill 1709, would bar certain online platforms from providing an “addictive feature” to users under 16 years old and add ways to verify users’ ages.
Under the bill, prohibited addictive features include autoplay and feeds that display recommended content.
The addictive nature of autoplay and other features is “harmful, full stop, and that they’re not appropriate for the developing brain,” said Lowenthal, who authored the bill.
Newsom, who chatted with lawmakers at the Capitol on Monday in what will be his last regular legislative session as governor, praised Lowenthal and the bill.
“I’m really proud of the work that we did together on that. My legislator of the year is Josh Lowenthal,” Newsom said. “California will continue to lead in this area as we must continue to lead in this area.”
After watching technology “run free” in California for years, legislators are now seeking to “pump the brakes a little bit,” said Samantha Vigil, a UC Davis researcher who built a registry tracking social media legislation in states across the country.
“They want to reevaluate what is working,” said Vigil. “What is healthy and beneficial, and what is progress just for the sake of having a new iteration of something?”
All 50 states have introduced or passed some type of digital media or technology-related legislation, tackling smartphone use in schools, social media and chatbots, Vigil said.
Other countries have taken more stringent steps to limit social media use among young people. Australia banned social media use for those under 16, but enforcing the law has been challenging because young people have tried to get around the restrictions.
California isn’t trying to ban social media; instead, it’s trying to limit how platforms design their features.
Parents and state attorneys general have not waited for policy makers to act. They have sued Meta, Google and other tech companies over the alleged harms their products have done to young people.
In late August, Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, agreed to pay up to $17 billion and make child-safety changes to resolve a multi-state lawsuit alleging the tech company designed and deployed harmful features while misleading the public about potential harms. Meta and YouTube also lost a social media addiction lawsuit earlier this year in Los Angeles.
Meta has agreed to pay $17 billion and add child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms to end a landmark trial over teen social media addiction and settle claims filed by 47 states
Assembly Bill 1709 goes further. For example, Meta’s settlement gives teens the option to pick a non-algorithmic feed and turn off autoplay but, unlike in the legislation, it’s not mandatory. The bill would also apply to other platforms outside of Meta. Meta declined to comment.
Tech industry and business group opposing the bill say it is too blunt and could cut off access to social media’s benefits, according to the bill’s analysis.
“The durable path is to enforce the targeted laws California already has and to strengthen parental tools rather than an overlapping framework whose scope can be redrawn by regulation,” said Robert Boykin, TechNet’s Executive Director for California and the Southwest.
California lawmakers passed another Lowenthal bill aimed at holding social media liable for harm caused to children. Under Assembly Bill 2, social media companies could face fines of up to $1 million per child for negligent harm.
California lawmakers this year also attempted to tackle two other perils of the technological world — the rapid development and implementation of artificial intelligence and the proliferation of the massive data centers that are essential to sustaining the AI universe.
National and state union leaders have urged California legislators and Newsom to protect workers from the threats of AI to replace workers, saying it posed an existential threat to the foundation of a healthy, productive democracy.
“AI must remain a tool controlled by humans, not the other way around,” said Sen. Jerry McNerney (D-Pleasanton).
The state Legislature on Monday approved McNerney’s bill, Senate Bill 947, which would bar employers from “solely” using automated decision-making systems to discipline or fire employees. If an employer primarily relies upon this system, a human must verify the decision.
Lawmakers also approved Senate Bill 951, introduced by Sen. Eloise Gomez Reyes (D-Colton), which would require employers to provide a 60-day advance notice to workers and local and state governments before AI-related layoffs. Lawmakers also approved Assembly Bill 1609, which requires large private businesses that serve customers to provide access to human customer service representatives and to disclose to use of chatbots.
They passed another bill by Sen. Steve Padilla (D-Chula Vista) that enacts a four-year moratorium on the sale and manufacturing of AI-chatbot powered toys over concerns that the technology can harm children.
On Friday, lawmakers agreed on a compromise on proposed legislation to regulate energy use by California’s growing data center industry, measures prompted by community fears about the massive complexes. Lawmakers say the legislation would help protect consumers from growing electricity costs driven upward by the sprawling facilities and to track the centers’ immense energy and water consumption.
At a June hearing on Senate Bill 886 to regulate data centers’ energy use, Assemblymember Pilar Schiavo (D-Chatsworth) said it’s just “a handful of companies that are gonna make trillions of dollars” from AI. They should pay for related utility infrastructure upgrades, she added.
“People, I would argue, are not even begging to use AI,” she said. “They’re struggling to figure it out to keep up with the times, but don’t even really want it.”
The California legislature is expected to vote on two of the bills to regulate the controversial industry within the next day.
Whether Newsom will embrace the legislature’s efforts to corral big Tech in California — in part of in whole — remains unclear.
Newsom last year vetoed a similar AI bill from McNerney to ban automated decision-making systems to discipline employees over worries that it could restrict companies’ ability to use customer ratings. That element was dropped in this year’s legislation.
Newsom last year signed Assembly Bill 56 that required social media platforms to display mental health warning labels to users under 18 starting in January 2027. But he also vetoed Senate Bill 771 that aimed to hold social media platforms liable if they amplified content that contributed to hate crimes and other violent acts, saying that the legislation was “premature” and current civil rights laws might be adequate.
Lowenthal said he’s heard from California families who are anxious about social media and seeking “relief” from their concerns about how the platforms are affecting their children.
“This is a kitchen-table topic,” he said. “I’ve yet to find a family with school-age children in the state of California, any corner of the state, that is not going through this right now.”
Times staff writer Taryn Luna contributed to this report.

articles.title: India needs to make up its mind about economic ties with China
articles.body:

India needs to make up its mind about economic ties with China
New Delhi’s approach has gone from welcoming economic engagement with Beijing to containment to the latest calibrated reopening
4-MIN READ4-MIN
2
 Listen
As India prepares for the Brics summit less than two weeks away, relations with China are warming up. On July 22, Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar met his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi during the East Asia Summit; five days later, Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri visited China. Last week, Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval also visited Beijing, for border talks.
But India remains deeply ambivalent when it comes to economic engagement with China: it seeks Chinese capital, technology and expertise while fearing the shocks they may bring. Justifying the latest economic engagement with China, Jaishankar said India’s long-term objective was to compete with China in manufacturing.
After six years of sweeping curbs on Chinese investment, bilateral trade rose to US$151.1 billion in the financial year ended March 31. China remains India’s largest import source and has, after four years, displaced the United States as its top trading partner. India’s approach to engaging with China has evolved: from welcoming participation to containment after 2020 and, more recently, a calibrated reopening.
During Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s first term and the early years of his second, India maintained a broadly open stance. Launched in 2014, the “Make in India” campaign sought to slash bureaucratic hurdles and attract foreign investment. During Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit that September, both sides signed a five-year economic cooperation plan. Modi’s 2015 China visit yielded a further US$22 billion in commercial deals.
Economic engagement remained robust even after the 2017 Doklam stand-off. Both sides maintained senior economic dialogue, pursued the “China India Plus One” approach to projects in third countries and planned connectivity projects. Chinese investment in Indian start-ups grew twelvefold between 2016 and 2019, backing at least 18 of India’s 30 unicorns. In 2019, China proposed a manufacturing partnership. By early 2020, the stock of Chinese investment in India was estimated to exceed US$26 billion.
But that was also the year the turning point came. In April, India introduced a requirement of prior government approval for foreign direct investment (FDI) from countries it shared a land border with, ostensibly to block “opportunistic takeovers”. After the deadly Galwan Valley border clash, restrictions against Chinese businesses expanded. India banned Chinese apps on national security grounds, tightened public procurement rules for bidders and required security clearance for directors from border countries. Visa delays, regulatory raids and other pressures suffocated Chinese business.

articles.title: Russian War Criminal Yan Petrovsky Gets 12-Year Prison Term — Previously Given Life Sentence
articles.body:
The Helsinki Court of Appeals has handed down a ruling in the war crimes case involving Russian national Yan Petrovsky, also known as Vojislav Torden.
This was reported by YLE.
The court sentenced Petrovsky to 12.5 years in prison for three war crimes, although he had previously faced a life sentence.
In March of last year, the Helsinki District Court sentenced the Russian man to life in prison for four war crimes committed in 2014 during an ambush in eastern Ukraine. According to the court, the most serious of these was the murder of a Ukrainian soldier.
In the appeals court, Petrovsky demanded that the charges be dismissed or, at the very least, that his sentence be reduced. Meanwhile, the prosecutor demanded that the Russian be convicted on five counts.
The Court of Appeals concluded that Petrovsky was not liable as a leader for organizing the ambush, which was carried out on September 5, 2014, using a Ukrainian flag.
The ambush against the Aidar battalion in the Luhansk region resulted in the deaths of 22 Ukrainian soldiers and injuries to four others. The Court of Appeals determined that at least four of the deceased had sustained injuries during the attack.
The court recognized that Petrovsky served as deputy commander of the Rusich group. In addition to the commander and his deputy, at least two other members of the group participated in the ambush.
The Russian national denied his role in the group and his participation in the ambush. At the same time, the court established that Petrovsky fired a light machine gun at Ukrainian servicemen, which was classified as a war crime.
However, according to the appeals court, there was insufficient evidence in the case to prove that Petrovsky himself or the two other members of the Rusich group fired at the wounded Ukrainian servicemen.
The appellate court also determined that Petrovsky, as a leader, is not liable for the shooting at wounded Ukrainian servicemen and therefore dismissed the charges on this count.
At the same time, the court recognized that, by participating in joint military operations with others, Petrovsky bears partial responsibility for the killing and wounding of Ukrainian servicemen.
Furthermore, the court ruled that the Russian did not commit a war crime by carving the Rusich group’s symbol into the cheek of a Ukrainian serviceman.
In the court’s view, the wound was superficial, did not cause bleeding, and the damage to the cheek was temporary. Therefore, these actions “did not cause severe physical or mental suffering, which is necessary for classification as a war crime.”
The Court of Appeals also ordered Petrovsky to pay compensation to the soldiers wounded during the ambush and to the relatives of those killed.
Petrovsky was detained in August 2023.

articles.title: Iceland just friend-zoned the EU
articles.body:
Iceland just friend-zoned the EU
Well, what do you know! It turns out that you really can crawl into bed with Brussels on your own terms, and be friends with benefits, all without the need to officially shack up. 
 The people of Iceland have just done something that would usually be considered political blasphemy here in Europe. They’ve decided that their country would like to remain in charge of itself, voting 53% to 47% in a referendum not to pursue getting officially hitched to the EU.
It’s a rarity these days to see a show of democracy that’s something other than just a midwife delivering whatever Brussels wants. It even had to be warned by elected officials not to meddle. Icelanders considered just the idea of continuing EU accession talks, which was the subject of this referendum – not even “do you want EU membership or not,” but only “should even we keep playing footsie with Brussels over it” – and decided that they didn’t need a ring on their finger in order to keep their toothbrush in Brussels’ bathroom.
Iceland already has access to the European common market through the European Economic Area (EEA). What else could it possibly gain from greater submission to Brussels that would actually make it worth surrendering any more of its autonomy?
Much has since been made of comparisons to the UK and Brexit, arguing that Iceland’s inclusion in the EU’s common market isn’t true independence and that if it were, then the UK wouldn’t have needed to withdraw from the EU entirely. But they’re comparing a bitter post-divorce Brexit deal with a country being wooed. Do you treat your ex-wife like your new girlfriend?
Iceland gets market access without becoming part of the EU’s full political and institutional machinery, with all the constraints and impositions that alone brings. EU law has primacy over its member states’ conflicting national law, which is a fundamentally different legal relationship from Iceland’s as a non-member. And then there’s the matter of Icelanders wanting to retain control over their country’s primary assets – fisheries and agriculture. It knows exactly what Brussels is eyeing up and down.
So basically, they’re saying, “Why would we voluntarily make ourselves less capable of deciding what happens here?” It probably doesn’t much help that the EU has developed a real talent for taking relatively straightforward questions and feeding them into a regulatory meat grinder to the point where nobody remembers what the original issue was.
Take packaging, as a recent example. Everyone voted on this nonsense requiring reusable containers for take-out in the same way that you have to show up to the supermarket with a reusable bag, or else risk having your groceries tumble out of your arms and into the crosswalk en route while returning home. (And forget about using a car, Earth-killer.) I guess nobody thought through what would happen once the measures actually took effect. Because the EU Commission, which drafted the nonsense, recently went like, “Wooo, boy! Exactly how high were we when we came up with this one?!” Then it urged member states not to enforce the rules or related penalties. That’s not exactly a compelling way to entice anyone to voluntarily hand over even more authority to these same jokers.
And Brussels understands that Iceland remains useful to the EU regardless. “The European Commission takes note of the outcome of Iceland’s referendum. The Commission respects the choice of the Icelandic people. Iceland remains a close partner of the European Union,” it said. In other words, “You may have declined our marriage proposal, but it’s not the end of our relationship.”
That’s something typically said when the declining party has something that you really want, to the point that you’re still willing to concede the dream of total control for the consolation prize of continued access.
The lesson here is that you really CAN cooperate with the EU without becoming fully absorbed by it, and you can trade with it without transferring every conceivable decision to it, and you can have common interests without having a common political identity that’s decided by bureaucrats, after which countries and citizens are squeezed into it like mental patients into a straitjacket.
Iceland has just proven that there’s a third option that exists between isolation and membership. The congratulations came from global sources as diverse as the populist right and left, and even globalist establishment crony and former US national security advisor John Bolton, who framed it as a rejection of Trump’s invasion-related fear-mongering that risked making Iceland feel insecure enough to run straight into the EU’s arms.
Folks from all sides seem to have actually accepted Icelanders saying no – even the EU, despite sounding as thrilled about it as a rejected guy getting up off his dusty knee, post-proposal. Usually, when people vote the ‘wrong’ way, we’re treated to lectures about misinformation, populism, Russian influence, democratic backsliding, or the possibility that the electorate has simply become too stupid to appreciate the wonderful plan being implemented on its behalf. But Iceland appears to have escaped this compulsory remedial democracy class. She’s just that hot, apparently.
Canada, in particular, should take note before getting too cozy with Brussels, because the EU is so thirsty for its natural resources these days, drooling over its ample natural assets while the mainstream Western press fantasizes en masse about a European-Canadian wedding.
Iceland is now the indisputable gold standard in geopolitical thirst trapping.
Sounds like a good time for the EU to ponder why its regulatory and bureaucratic smooth moves aren’t proving enough to seal the deal when the average citizen actually gets a say.
